General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople.
  • Industry observers note that I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since.
  • It has been revealed that you didn’t fail the program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

Industry observers note that I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

It has been revealed that you didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

It has been revealed that the reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

It has been revealed that nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

According to recent reports, now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

According to recent reports, the veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

In a recent development, we do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

It has been revealed that that work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

According to recent reports, we haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

In a recent development, if you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

Industry observers note that we’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

It has been revealed that lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

Tech Report: Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that can AI time savings be measured?
  • This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s newly introduced monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.
  • Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s newly introduced monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

Recent findings suggest that “Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

Recent findings suggest that the time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Sources indicate that debt was a major part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and noted the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the manufacturer said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Recent findings suggest that instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”.

Sources indicate that the announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first unveiled in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

In a recent development, “Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner remarked in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”.

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

#99210. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • Recent findings suggest that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

Industry observers note that the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Recent findings suggest that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

Industry observers note that “For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” mentioned Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

According to recent reports, millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another massive expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

According to recent reports, baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

It has been revealed that but their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

Industry observers note that “The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

Recent findings suggest that that dynamic demonstrates up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners remarked they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

It has been revealed that this analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

According to recent reports, monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

It has been revealed that income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

It has been revealed that share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report demonstrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Industry observers note that yingqi is a Senior Economist at Redfin. He studies housing market trends and explains what’s driving them for a broad audience. He previously led research on responsible AI at Freddie Mac, and also worked at Meta and the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Yingqi holds a Ph.D. in economics from Georgetown University, and his research is published in the American Economic Journal: Microeconomics and the Journal of Real Estate Finance and Economics.

Anthropic’s Siren tests whether Claude models will break out of an insecure sandbox

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at artificial intelligence developer Anthropic PBC today published details on Siren, a new evaluation that tests whether AI agents will break out of an insecure sandbox to get at something that would help them complete a task.
  • The researchers found that recent Claude models will reach outside the sandbox in about a fifth to a third of Siren’s test scenarios, though they are far less likely than earlier models to then make misaligned use of what they find.
  • Siren has been part of Anthropic’s system cards since the release of Claude Haiku 5.5 in October, with the company also using it as one input when deciding whether to deploy new models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:56 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Researchers at artificial intelligence developer Anthropic PBC today published details on Siren, a new evaluation that tests whether AI agents will break out of an insecure sandbox to get at something that would help them complete a task.

The researchers found that recent Claude models will reach outside the sandbox in about a fifth to a third of Siren’s test scenarios, though they are far less likely than earlier models to then make misaligned use of what they find.

Siren has been part of Anthropic’s system cards since the release of Claude Haiku 5.5 in October, with the company also using it as one input when deciding whether to deploy new models.

Recent findings suggest that siren includes 26 sandbox environments built from five common setups, such as bubblewrap jails, Docker containers and small virtual machines emulated with QEMU. Because they show up most often in public reports of sandbox escapes, misconfigurations make up most of the weaknesses planted in the environments.

While the model works on a routine DevOps task, a honeypot such as a credential or file that would help it finish the job is placed outside the sandbox. What Anthropic calls “tempters” are then layered on top to make the honeypot harder to resist. None of the tempters gives the model permission to leave the sandbox, according to the company.

Industry observers note that across Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Mythos 5.2, misaligned use came in at 0.6% to 1.6% of scenarios. Anthropic defines that as using the outside material in a way no reasonable reading of the scenario allows.

Sources indicate that the earlier Mythos 5.1 and Mythos 5 models were much higher, at 12.7% and 25.8%. According to Anthropic, Siren’s rates are not an estimate of real-world use, since the evaluation is designed to make the behavior easy to measure. All of the models were also tested without the safeguards that ship with its released models.

Along with Siren itself, Anthropic detailed three ways to make an escape less likely. Adding a short description of the sandbox to the system prompt, including six rules for staying inside it and an instruction to stop if a task needs something the model was not given, made each model 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside. Giving the model a tool to report sandbox weaknesses to the people who run the sandbox also helped, cutting the rate of reaching outside by 7 to 33 percentage points.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic also put auto mode, a feature in many of its products that uses a classifier to check tool calls before they run, through an offline replay of the Siren episodes. Auto mode blocked the first command that read the honeypot in 96% to 100% of misaligned uses, though the tech giant cautions that it tuned the classifier’s rules on those same episodes.

Industry observers note that with all three mitigations running, misaligned use fell to zero in five of the six models tested, with Mythos 5 at 0.1%. The tradeoff was that two models completed about nine percentage points fewer of the tasks that could be finished inside the sandbox. According to Anthropic, none of the mitigations fixes the sandbox itself.

The research follows Anthropic’s disclosure in July that three Claude models had gained unauthorized access to the systems of three organizations while being run through cybersecurity evaluations. The manufacturer blamed a misconfigured evaluation environment that had been left with live internet access.

Brian Soby, co-founder and chief executive of AI agent supervision startup Pretxt Inc., which introduced last week with $5 million in seed funding, told SiliconANGLE that Siren is “an attempt to harden sandboxes, but that is ultimately a flawed protection approach.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Sandboxes attempt to contain the impact of a misaligned model. But misalignment is the core matter,” Soby said. “Increasingly clever models have repeatedly demonstrated the ineffectiveness of the sandboxing concept and the serious consequences of relying on containment to overcome fundamental misalignment.”.

Soby likened sandboxing to “prison labor,” in which low trust means stripping workers of most of their capabilities and access. A far more effective approach, he mentioned, is active supervision that keeps agents aligned with their role and an organization’s rules.

Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.
  • Recent findings suggest that existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million).
  • Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun remarked mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

According to recent reports, “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun mentioned in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant stated in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

Recent findings suggest that “So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant stated. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Industry observers note that added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

In a recent development, “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he mentioned. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

Industry observers note that “If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale noted existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

Industry observers note that “Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale stated jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she noted. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun mentioned rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he noted. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the major change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

According to recent reports, however, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

Industry observers note that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on latest pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

It has been revealed that on this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel vital.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Industry observers note that shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy indicates many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

In a recent development, for agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

According to recent reports, his advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm.

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder stated he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios revealed Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos stated a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos stated the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

Sources indicate that “By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”.

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

Sources indicate that “We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he remarked. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

According to recent reports, last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

Recent findings suggest that the Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

In a recent development, finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Recent findings suggest that investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are Fresh York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Iowa Residents Told To Evacuate or Shelter in Place as U.S. Army Prepares To Detonate Nearly 10,000 Pounds of a Lead Explosive

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Army aims to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.
  • In a recent development, the detonation is scheduled to go ahead at 10 a.m.
  • Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the looks were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Army aims to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in Southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups.

In a recent development, the detonation is scheduled to go ahead at 10 a.m. on Wednesday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, IA. This comes after a lawsuit was filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter asking the federal appeals court to halt the plan.

Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the looks were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization.

It has been revealed that set to be detonated are 68 drums of degraded lead azide, adding up to roughly 9,700 pounds, which have become sensitive and unstable. It is the primary explosive used to initiate munitions.

A controlled detonation is now the only viable option, according to the Army’s Q&A page about the event.

As lead azide degrades, it crystalizes and becomes sensitive to temperature changes, shock, and friction, making it unsafe to move. There are chemical neutralization procedures, but the drums are too unstable for the physical manipulation this option requires, according to the Army.

In a recent development, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 7 Director Jim Macy wrote a letter to Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, ensuring her that the EPA was working alongside the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Defense to ensure the controlled detonation was “conducted in the safest manner possible.”.

“All agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” Macy wrote in the letter, according to the Iowa Capital Dispatch.

An updated public safety advisory shared by the Army on Tuesday shared the agency’s looks to make the detonation as safe as possible. The lead azide will be detonated in earth-covered magazines, which are built for the purposes of holding ammunition and explosives, and are reinforced.

Sources indicate that additional physical barriers made of sand, a “water wall,” gel blocks, and aqueous foam barriers will be in place to contain particle dispersion, absorb thermal energy, and reduce airborne particulate dispersal. These measures, as well as drone surveillance of lead levels, are in place to track and minimize deposition outside the plant.

Industry observers note that the Army has acknowledged that lead particles will impact communities outside the plant. It has defined an evacuation zone as a "5-mile cone extending southwest of IAAAP.".

Those in the evacuation zone will be provided short-term hotel lodging, food, water, and transportation as needed.

It has also laid out recommendations for those outside the evacuation zone, such as sheltering in place, closing all windows and doors, and setting heating to recirculate and avoid pulling in air from outside.

Still, environmental groups are concerned about the lead plume, which they say could spread 100 miles, depending on weather conditions.

"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," noted Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, in a press release shared with Realtor.com®.

"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal.".

Sources indicate that the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, Iowa Chapter, were only made aware of the unprecedented detonation strategy early last week, initially scheduled for Friday. In response, the groups filed a lawsuit on Thursday challenging the permit that the EPA issued the Army.

“Based on the information that was made public at the time, which was very little information, there were serious concerns about the effectiveness of the public notification and the information being put out to protect the public,” Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earth Justice, tells Realtor.com.

“There were serious concerns about the mitigations measures in place to reduce the impact as well as to properly do remediation and cleanup and address any harm that people may face from the impact of the detonation.”.

Many local lawmakers were not made aware of the controlled detonation either, and were only informed about the plans and risk once the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra club told them, despite the widespread impact on surrounding communities, according to Chau.

“That’s why we filed the lawsuit: to make sure that all the information and resources and capabilities that could be provided were provided to the people potentially impacted by this,” indicates Chau.

In a recent development, “Since that filing, a lot of things have happened. The government has put out a lot more information, and while we expect a detonation to take place this Wednesday, we are glad to see that because there was additional time, there are now additional mitigation measures and resources have been provided for potentially impacted people.”.

Industry observers note that the Department of Justice responded in opposition to the lawsuit. Both the DOJ and Army maintain that a controlled detonation is the safest option and further delay, especially with cold weather approaching, could lead to a natural, uncontrolled detonation, which would be more difficult to mitigate.

“The Army has delayed detonation by three days now,” the DOJ’s brief said. “But every day of delay increases the risk of an uncontrolled explosion that will cause far greater public health and environmental harm than the planned, controlled detonation initiated under the protective terms of the Permit.”.

Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, intends Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.
  • Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, revealed a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

Sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, revealed a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the tech giant plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

Industry observers note that sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

Industry observers note that “This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

According to recent reports, while the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky stated. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The organization must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Industry observers note that group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently declared intends for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our manufacturer’s history,” he mentioned.

The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

Recent findings suggest that “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky said. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft Corp.
  • Sources indicate that the outage on Nov.
  • In a memo to staff on Friday, Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, described the outage as the most customer-affecting incident in the history of Exchange Online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:44 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft Corp. has declared an internal “Code Red” to overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures following the nearly 24-hour outage that took down Exchange Online and other Microsoft 365 services earlier this month, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters today.

Sources indicate that the outage on Nov. 12 and 13 also disrupted Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence assistant, affecting governments from Australia and Japan to the U.S., delaying trading firms and disrupting airline communications. The designation signals the most severe and urgent level of alert inside Microsoft, according to the report.

In a memo to staff on Friday, Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft 365 Core, described the outage as the most customer-affecting incident in the history of Exchange Online. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson wrote. He also conceded that the work done over the years had not been enough to protect the company on the day of the outage.

Engineers working the incident faced a “fog of war,” according to a separate memo sent on Monday by Amanda Silver, corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ. Silver’s memo describes responders exchanging more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, with diagnostic data spread across fragmented internal tracking systems.

The Code Red covers five workstreams set out by Silver, including load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft has also set a target of resolving future incidents worldwide within an hour, with AI agents to be used to help engineers diagnose system health data more promptly.

In a recent development, how long it takes to push out fixes is another concern raised by Henderson. Writing in an earlier memo this month, Henderson noted one urgent production fix had taken five to six days to reach worldwide saturation, while for urgent security issues the goal is to go from detection to safe worldwide deployment within an hour, something he admitted the organization has yet to achieve. Henderson also aims to hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team that oversees the engineering group responsible for the underlying Microsoft 365 services, along with weekly reviews of the corrective work.

Recent findings suggest that the outage itself was blamed by Microsoft on a defect introduced in July in a fix that had been prepared for its Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. Under certain load conditions, lock contention inside an internal Windows process was found to exhaust processor and memory resources on the servers, leaving more than 80% of them unresponsive at the worst point, according to Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report. Microsoft, whose Chief Executive Satya Nadella has publicly apologized for the disruption, has remarked the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents.

Silver’s memo also cites Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, who told a Code Red review that the affected component had seen “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”.

Speed comes with its own risks, according to security experts. “What concerns me is that speed and safety pull against each other,” Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering at AI security operations startup Secure.com, told SiliconANGLE. In his view, a pipeline able to push a fix to the world in an hour “can push a mistake in an hour.”.

Geographic traffic partitioning, which Ahmed stated limits how far a single bad change can travel, is the one of the five Code Red workstreams he would be watching.

Darin Fredde, senior director and offensive security evangelist at autonomous penetration testing company Ridge Security Technology Inc., noted that “an organization may have a recovery plan but still struggle to execute it if the tools needed to recover depend on the service that has failed.”.

The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients.
  • According to recent reports, ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place.
  • Industry observers note that wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

According to recent reports, ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Industry observers note that wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

It has been revealed that that shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an notable question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Industry observers note that today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

Sources indicate that A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

Industry observers note that at The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

It has been revealed that start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Sources indicate that invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

Sources indicate that as brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle firm talked about building for years but always found too significant to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting newly introduced software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle firm talked about building for years but always found too significant to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting newly introduced software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

It has been revealed that “The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” mentioned Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how massive we’re willing to dream.”.

Recent findings suggest that the ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The firm has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy noted there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he noted. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

According to recent reports, pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The newly introduced products take that approach further:.

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Industry observers note that duffy noted he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” stated Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy stated.

In a recent development, AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy noted. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

It has been revealed that duffy mentioned many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The latest products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of firm: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The upcoming products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

In a recent development, “This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy noted. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

It has been revealed that bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Sources indicate that neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy stated.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the organization’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy remarked. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Sources indicate that duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the organization, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy stated, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

According to recent reports, about 40 of the tech giant’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy remarked Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Industry observers note that despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the organization, Duffy mentioned Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

In a recent development, asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy stated Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

It has been revealed that the October jobs report indicated employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

Industry observers note that the gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

It has been revealed that at October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

In a recent development, the Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh stated in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Industry observers note that adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS mentioned a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

Sources indicate that the number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

Sources indicate that the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

In a recent development, forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

#99194. If the AI Bubble Pops, Here’s What It Means for Your Home’s Value
