#99156. Industry News: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1537 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

In a recent development, ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Fresh York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He stated he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, mentioned music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be stated for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

According to recent reports, megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

According to recent reports, “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan noted. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Industry observers note that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

It has been revealed that “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

In a recent development, agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

In a recent development, sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

According to recent reports, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

According to recent reports, natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she stated, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova remarked. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

Sources indicate that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

In a recent development, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

According to recent reports, andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She states music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he states, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

According to recent reports, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

It has been revealed that rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

In a recent development, “In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer noted. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

According to recent reports, shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea states she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

It has been revealed that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

It has been revealed that his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein noted.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

In a recent development, “Every week, I share latest songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he mentioned. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Sources indicate that bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she mentioned.

In a recent development, as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova stated she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

UPDATED 20:41 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Employees working at frontier artificial intelligence model companies Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC have been butting heads with executives over advanced models whose reasoning is such that the models pose to danger to humanity, according to a report by Axios today based on more than two dozen sources familiar with the current standoff at the companies.

The report states the models in question are far more powerful than anything that has so far reached the public, showing great leaps forward in reasoning in many areas that have been difficult, “if not impossible,” to control during tests. It appears that some staff err on the side of caution and believe the training should stop completely while others believe they can be reined in.

Recent findings suggest that “If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us… they will in fact be able to trick us successfully,” one of the researchers told Axios. “And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.”.

According to recent reports, after Open AI’s AI agents seemingly went berserk earlier this year and hacked the open-source AI platform Hugging Face Inc., there have been calls to pause AI development until safety can be assured. The state of California this month launched a lawsuit calling Open AI a “public nuisance,” whose models right now pose cybersecurity risks while threatening the “well-being of society.”.

The debate on how far we should go before we step on the brakes has largely been overshadowed by companies, and the countries where they are developed, steaming ahead winning the AI race. In the Axios report, many of the anonymous claimed executives are “out of touch” with safety challenges as they put profit first.

Recent findings suggest that nonetheless, Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei has been vocal about the “existential risks to humanity” that AI might bring. In his recent essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier,” Amodei stated “pacing” is key, warning that authoritarian regimes such as China must agree to cooperate in moving forward slowly with the frontier models. President Trump has been less than supportive of such measures, calling the threats to humanity a “hoax.”.

Industry observers note that larry Xiangdong Chen, the Manufacturer's founder, Chairman and CEO, commented, "This quarter, our net revenues increased by 18.3% year over year to nearly RMB1.9 billion, and we achieved GAAP operating profitability in a third quarter for the first time. Our performance reflects solid improvements in resource allocation and management efficiency, alongside our continued focus on high-quality products and services. Deeper integration of AI and digital tools also elevated efficiency across teaching, services, and operations. This enabled us to unlock operating leverage while maintaining high delivery standards, enhancing the scalability of our business model and strengthening our long-term earnings potential. We also remain committed to returning value to shareholders: as of November 24, 2026, we had repurchased approximately RMB780.5 million under our aggregated share repurchase programs.

It has been revealed that 'One Customer Commitment' defines how we serve learners across different stages of life. Our comprehensive product portfolio empowers us to accompany owners throughout their learning journeys, and the trust we earn through every high-quality delivery is what keeps them choosing Gaotu at each step of their growth. Over time, this trust will strengthen our competitive advantage and support sustainable value creation for shareholders. ".

Robin Bin Luo, COO of the Organization, added, "Profitable growth remained our focus in the third quarter, guiding our resource allocation strategy and dynamic adjustments across products and channels. Gains in user acquisition efficiency were a key driver of operating margin expansion, underscoring stronger execution in product selection, channel management, and cost control. We also continued to refine our business portfolio, concentrating resources on businesses with clear market demand, differentiated competitive strengths, and attractive operating returns. As businesses with stronger unit economics contribute a growing share of revenue, we expect to see greater operating leverage, supporting more sustainable growth and improved profitability.".

Financial Results for the Third Quarter of 2026.

It has been revealed that net revenues increased by 18.3% to RMB1,868.4 million from RMB1,579.0 million in the third quarter of 2025, which was primarily driven by continued year-over-year growth in gross billings as a result of our sufficient and effective response to the strong market demand. Our high-quality educational products and learning services also gained wider recognition of our product and service offerings.

It has been revealed that cost of revenues increased by 18.1% to RMB632.2 million from RMB535.5 million in the third quarter of 2025. The increase was mainly due to the expansion of instructors and tutors workforce, increased server and bandwidth cost, higher rental cost, and increased learning materials cost.

Gross profit increased by 18.5% to RMB1,236.2 million from RMB1,043.5 million in the third quarter of 2025. Gross profit margin increased to 66.2% from 66.1% in the same period of 2025.

Non-GAAP gross profit increased by 18.4% to RMB1,236.7 million from RMB1,044.5 million in the third quarter of 2025. Non-GAAP gross profit margin increased to 66.2% from 66.1% in the same period of 2025.

Operating expenses increased by 1.1% to RMB1,235.1 million from RMB1,221.5 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Income from operations was RMB1.1 million, compared with loss from operations of RMB178.0 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Non-GAAP income from operations was RMB8.5 million, compared with non-GAAP loss from operations of RMB168.6 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Interest Income, Net and Realized Gains from Investments.

Interest income, net and realized gains from investments, in the aggregate, were RMB9.6 million, compared with a total of RMB14.9 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Other income, net was RMB4.1 million, compared with other income, net of RMB14.6 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Net income was RMB15.6 million, compared with net loss of RMB147.1 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Non-GAAP net income was RMB23.1 million, compared with non-GAAP net loss of RMB137.7 million in the third quarter of 2025.

Net operating cash outflow in the third quarter of 2026 was RMB794.8 million.

Basic and Diluted Net Income per ADS.

Basic and diluted net income per ADS were both RMB0.07 in the third quarter of 2026.

Non-GAAP basic and diluted net income per ADS were both RMB0.10 in the third quarter of 2026.

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had 155,503,808 ordinary shares outstanding.

Cash and Cash Equivalents, Restricted Cash, Short-term and Long-term Investments.

As of September 30, 2026, the Organization had cash and cash equivalents, restricted cash, short-term and long-term investments of RMB3,128.0 million in aggregate, compared with a total of RMB3,972.5 million as of December 31, 2025.

In November 2022, the Tech giant's board of directors authorized a share repurchase program ("2022 Share Repurchase Program"), under which the Company may repurchase up to US$30 million of its shares, effective until November 22, 2025. In November 2023, the Company's board of directors authorized modifications to the share repurchase program, increasing the aggregate value of shares that may be repurchased from US$30 million to US$80 million, effective until November 22, 2025.

As of September 22, 2025, the Tech giant's repurchase amount had reached US$80 million and the 2022 Share Repurchase Program was completed.

In May 2025, the Company's board of directors authorized a newly introduced share repurchase program ("2025 Share Repurchase Program"), under which the Company may repurchase up to an aggregate value of US$100 million of its shares during the three-year period beginning upon the completion of the Company's 2022 Share Repurchase Program.

As of November 24, 2026, the Company had cumulatively repurchased approximately 39.0 million ADSs for approximately US$109.3 million under the aforesaid two share repurchase programs.

These estimates reflect the Company's current expectations, which are subject to change.

About Non-GAAP Financial Measures.

The Company uses gross billings, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP income (loss) from operations and non-GAAP net income (loss), each a non-GAAP financial measure, in evaluating its operating results and for financial and operational decision-making purposes.

In a recent development, the Organization defines gross billings for a specific period as the total amount of cash received for the sale of course offerings in such period, net of the total amount of refunds in such period. The Company's management uses gross billings as a performance measurement because the Company generally bills its students for the entire course fee at the time of sale of its course offerings and recognizes revenue proportionally as the classes are delivered. For some courses, the Company continues to provide students with 12 months to 36 months access to the pre-recorded audio-video courses after the online live courses are delivered. The Company believes that gross billings provide valuable insight into the sales of its course packages and the performance of its business. As gross billings have material limitations as an analytical metrics and may not be calculated in the same manner by all companies, it may not be comparable to other similarly titled measures used by other companies.

In a recent development, non-GAAP gross profit, non-GAAP income (loss) from operations and non-GAAP net income (loss) exclude share-based compensation expenses. The Tech giant believes that these non-GAAP financial measures provide meaningful supplemental information regarding its performance and liquidity by excluding share-based expenses that may not be indicative of its operating performance from a cash perspective. The Company believes that both management and investors benefit from these non-GAAP financial measures in assessing its performance and when planning and forecasting future periods. These non-GAAP financial measures also facilitate management's internal comparisons to the Company's historical performance. A limitation of using non-GAAP measures is that these non-GAAP measures exclude share-based compensation charges that have been and will continue to be for the foreseeable future a significant recurring expense in the Company's business.

It has been revealed that the presentation of these non-GAAP financial measures is not intended to be considered in isolation from or as a substitute for the financial information prepared and presented in accordance with GAAP. Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

In a recent development, P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026.

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

It has been revealed that krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”.

Recent findings suggest that that opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

Recent findings suggest that VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The manufacturer confirmed Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it notes can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is right now in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Latest Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

Recent findings suggest that the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Recent findings suggest that companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon noted it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the manufacturer wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Upcoming York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

According to recent reports, amazon released its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel remarked the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

In a recent development, “We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel stated. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The manufacturer also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

Sources indicate that the standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled looks to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its looks for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time highlighted most Latest Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6.

According to recent reports, city leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Fresh Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company remarked it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

Breaking: What will Social Security look like in 2027 and beyond?

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, swiftly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.
  • In a recent development, earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently confirmed 3.6% COLA for 2027.
  • Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, swiftly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.

In a recent development, earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently confirmed 3.6% COLA for 2027. But Morningstar noted this week that the 2027 COLA — the largest since 2023’s 8.7% adjustment — will translate into smaller take-home increases once Medicare costs are deducted.

Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks. Morningstar reported that the standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 next year to $209.40, a 3.2% increase. That will allow most beneficiaries to keep more than 3% of the 3.6% COLA after the deduction.

Morningstar calculated that a retiree receiving the average October benefit of $2,092 would see a net benefit increase of about 3.29%, assuming they pay the standard Part B premium and have no other changes in deductions. A higher-income retiree with a $3,500 monthly benefit would see a net increase of roughly 3.41% under the same assumptions.

The COLA is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which compares the average readings for July, August and September on a year-over-year basis. Analysts cited by Morningstar noted that CPI-W may understate seniors’ actual cost pressures, particularly for healthcare, and pointed to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ CPI-E index for older households, which has historically risen faster than CPI-W.

The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) said the projected 3.6% COLA for 2028 is likely to arrive against a deteriorating backdrop for older adults, including senior homeowners who may still be making monthly mortgage payments. The group said that seniors are now the country’s fastest-growing homeless population and that many forgo vision, dental and hearing care due to costs.

TSCL’s release emphasized that Social Security’s primary trust fund is projected to reach insolvency in 2032, triggering automatic benefit reductions if Congress does not act. The Medicare Part A hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, the group mentioned.

Industry observers note that that timing elevates the stakes for the next Congress, which will be led by Democrats after their decisive victories in the recent midterm elections. Senators elected in the current cycle will serve from Jan. 3, 2027, through Jan. 3, 2033, overlapping the projected insolvency date. TSCL framed these terms as a key window for any reforms to prevent automatic benefit cuts for millions of retirees.

In its agenda for the 120th Congress, TSCL called on lawmakers to:.

Sources indicate that TSCL pointed to Social Security Administration projections, which show that eliminating the taxable wage cap would add “decades” to the trust fund’s life. And the organization’s internal polling indicates broad bipartisan support among seniors for lifting the cap.

As advocacy groups push for revenue-raising reforms, a upcoming proposal in the Senate would instead rely on federal borrowing to preserve full benefits.

According to recent reports, ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, has introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act. The bill would allow the Department of the Treasury to transfer general fund dollars to Social Security’s retirement trust fund once it becomes insolvent, according to a press release published last week by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB).

Sources indicate that under current law, Social Security can only pay benefits from dedicated payroll tax income and trust fund reserves. When the retirement trust fund’s reserves are exhausted — currently projected to be in less than six years — benefits would be cut by about 22% without legislative changes.

CRFB estimated that backfilling Social Security with general revenue under Johnson’s bill would increase federal debt by $190 trillion over the next 75 years on an inflation-adjusted basis, equal to roughly 165% of gross domestic product.

“Paying for Social Security out of the general fund would absolutely explode the national debt, costing a whopping 165% of GDP over 75 years before even considering the economic implications,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas stated in the release, arguing that the policy could trigger a debt crisis or unsettle bond markets even before it is fully implemented.

CRFB characterized the bill as avoiding “the real decisions” needed to repair Social Security’s finances and urged lawmakers to pursue a mix of adjustments — potentially through a bipartisan commission — that would close the program’s funding gap without shifting the shortfall onto the federal balance sheet.

The trajectory of Social Security and Medicare benefits has direct implications for housing demand and credit risk among the senior segment.

Net benefit increases closer to 3% than 3.6% may constrain seniors’ ability to absorb higher housing costs — including the required property tax, insurance and association dues associated with reverse mortgages. The impact could be particularly acute in housing markets with rapid property tax growth.

Recent findings suggest that rising healthcare and prescription costs could drive more senior homeowners to tap their equity through home sales or reverse mortgages. Increased levels of downsizing would alter inventory and product mixes in senior-heavy markets.

A 22% across-the-board benefit cut in the next decade, if Congress fails to act, would likely raise delinquency risks among fixed-income borrowers and could affect investor views of senior-heavy mortgage-backed securities pools. Conversely, large-scale borrowing to backfill Social Security, as proposed in Johnson’s bill, could influence interest rates and broader funding conditions.

According to recent reports, localized affordability pressures could also emerge. Growth in senior homelessness and medical cost burdens might increase demand for affordable and supportive housing. It could also influence municipal planning, tax policy and zoning decisions that shape housing development pipelines.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has declared a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the company’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In a recent development, in August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals announced a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, said today in a news release.

Sources indicate that “By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith remarked. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”.

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the firm’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas stated.

UPDATED 20:54 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure firm from its rival VMware Inc.

In a letter to firm employees, Ramaswami (pictured) said he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.

Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

In a recent development, “Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this tech giant and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”.

According to recent reports, ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the firm delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

The firm reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

Nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the firm guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

Recent findings suggest that investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

Recent findings suggest that virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the manufacturer during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she noted. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami stated he believes the tech giant is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

Industry observers note that “[We have] transformed the manufacturer to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami remarked. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”.

Sources indicate that according to Ramaswami, Nutanix now stands at an inflection point as it looks to cash in on the fresh era of artificial intelligence. “I’ve been talking to the board for a bit about this, as well as in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession, and so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time,” he told analysts. “[We wanted] to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader.”.

According to recent reports, ramaswami’s departure from the organization should at least be a lot smoother than his arrival. Nutanix announced it had appointed Ramaswami as its CEO in late 2020, just two days after he quit his role as chief operating officer of its biggest rival, VMware.

VMware was indignant about the manner of his departure, and responded with a lawsuit that accused Ramaswami of breaching his legal and contractual duties to the company by “secretly meeting” with Nutanix’s board to discuss taking over, while continuing to play a leading role in shaping its product and business strategy. The lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court about a year later.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. However, while the industry still doesn’t know exactly what the final rules will look like, it just moved a step closer to finding out.

Sources indicate that monday marked the end of the U.S. Department of the Treasury‘s public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban. Although ROAD explicitly exempted BTR from the ban, some of the proposed rules and language Treasury released in October have left the industry uneasy and unsure of where it stands.

BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into fresh projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules.

Sources indicate that last month, Treasury released a notice of proposed rulemaking detailing how it would implement the institutional investor ban while protecting BTR communities. The proposed rules would exempt newly built, never-owner-occupied BTR communities if an investor buys them within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy and uses them only as rentals.

Sources indicate that treasury would also exempt communities that include both rental and for-sale homes, allowing builders to sell the rental portion to large institutional investors while marketing the remaining homes to individual buyers. The proposals additionally call for allowing transfers of existing BTR communities between large institutional investors and keeping the renovate-to-rent exemption.

Although the rules appear to protect BTR, industry leaders say the finer details leave several concerns unresolved.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, mentioned in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Over the last month, Treasury received more than 450 letters with questions and concerns concerning its proposed rulemakings. HousingWire TBD reviewed 10 of those letters, from high-profile BTR developers and operators and leading organizations that advocate on behalf of the rental housing industry, including:.

In a recent development, these letters detailed the outstanding concerns that the industry still has concerning how Treasury will enforce ROAD. With the institutional investor ban set to take effect on January 7, Treasury has several weeks to finalize and release the rules that BTR operators will have to follow.

Until then, the industry has to wait and see whether, and how, those concerns are addressed.

Sources indicate that the chief concern among BTR developers, operators and advocates is the proposed requirement that institutional investors purchase BTR communities within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy (CO). Under the proposed framework, if a developer fails to sell a community by that deadline, they may lose the ability to do so altogether.

That proposal matters because many BTR developers, much like multifamily developers, rely on selling their communities after completion and stabilization to make a profit and move on to their next project.

Richard Ross, CEO at Quinn Residences, argued that the 18-month window is far too limiting. A community may still be under development and lease-up after the first homes receive a CO, so 18 months will almost certainly run out before the full community is ready to sell.

Recent findings suggest that “To build and stabilize a upcoming community takes about 30 months. If I start receiving certificates of occupancy at month 15, I may not receive the final CO for the last home until month 28 or 29. I need enough time to complete and stabilize the entire community before selling it,” Ross said in an interview.

The letters that HousingWire TBD reviewed unanimously opposed the proposed 18-month window. Just like Ross, industry groups argued that the deadline does not align with how rental communities are developed, leased up, financed and sold.

The letter signed by a coalition of 12 BTR developers led by Greystar and Brookfield Residential argued that the deadline would create uncertainty for projects that may not be sold until years after construction. The letter further argued the restrictions would continue to affect financing decisions for future projects.

“A smaller potential buyer pool reduces liquidity and creates greater uncertainty regarding terminal value,” the letter read.

Industry observers note that additionally, the groups argued that Treasury must protect long-term institutional owners’ ability to purchase BTR communities. Otherwise, the federal government would undermine the industry.

“If large institutional investors cannot purchase horizontal multifamily communities (which individual families cannot), the values of those properties will fall and latest construction and necessary maintenance and reinvestment will slow,” MBA’s letter read.

To address this, NAA and NMHC, two of the largest rental housing advocacy organizations, requested that Treasury eliminate the deadline or replace it with a provision that institutional investors can purchase BTR communities directly from the builder or developer responsible for construction.

Sources indicate that quinn Residences, AHV Communities and LGI Homes also requested that Treasury remove or substantially extend the deadline. LGI Homes also emphasized the need for production homebuilders to retain the option of renting homes that have not sold.

In a recent development, treasury’s proposed rulemaking describes the three activities that could qualify an institutional investor as a covered entity as “purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains”. This matters because BTR developers often build and retain homes as rental properties before selling stabilized communities to finance future developments.

Treasury’s language is ambiguous, leaving open the possibility that BTR developers could be treated like institutional investors.

It has been revealed that the National Rental Home Council made this a central argument in its letter, distinguishing between an investor buying a home from someone else and one acting as the builder. The organization urged Treasury to recognize that developers who build and retain homes as rentals operate differently from investors who purchase newly built homes from third parties.

Up for Growth Action made a similar argument, urging Treasury to differentiate between creating new rental housing and acquiring existing housing.

Several letters argued that Treasury’s proposed rule does not clearly distinguish single-plat rental communities, where multiple homes share one parcel and common ownership, from individual single-family homes. They worry the rule could inadvertently restrict the development, ownership or sale of these communities by treating them as collections of individual homes subject to the institutional investor ban.

In response, BTR advocates argued for clearer rules for single-plat communities and those mixing renters and owners, while NRHC asked whether buildings with three or more attached units could count as single-family homes.

The letters also raise concerns about the proposed exception for investors that purchase distressed homes, substantially rehabilitate them and rent them out. Treasury’s proposed rules would allow institutional investors to purchase existing homes in need of extensive repairs, as long as they spend 15% of the purchase price on improvements.

In a recent development, however, several of the letters argued that the 15% threshold is too high. They further argued that the rule could be hard to enforce for homes that are difficult to inspect before purchase, homes in jurisdictions without applicable local codes, and homes with problems that aren’t obvious upfront.

According to recent reports, rental housing advocates disagreed on how flexible the rehabilitation threshold should be. While some groups advocated for increasing the threshold, NMHC, NAA and RETTC support the 15% benchmark while advocating for more flexibility in identifying problems and applying older building standards.

The common theme is that industry leaders want the exception to work for genuinely distressed properties without requiring investors to predict every hidden problem before purchasing a home.

Several letters raise implementation problems beyond those five main concerns, including:.

Industry News: NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint noted he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

It has been revealed that white also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton mentioned it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or strategy.”.

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Sources indicate that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears mentioned the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

According to recent reports, “John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” mentioned David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

According to recent reports, pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

It has been revealed that “Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am.

Orchard Robotics, an agtech manufacturer using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was announced Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

Industry observers note that the startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, mentioned in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

Sources indicate that “Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu noted in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

According to recent reports, the startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

It has been revealed that orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round revealed in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

In a recent development, the Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

  • This decision comes after over a year of regulatory filings and multiple delays.
  • Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Investment firm Roundhill has suddenly terminated aims to launch two new XRP- and Solana (SOL)-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

This decision comes after over a year of regulatory filings and multiple delays.

As per the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings on Nov. 18, Roundhill has officially withdrawn plans to launch the Roundhill XRP Covered Call Strategy ETF and Roundhill Solana Covered Call Strategy ETF.

Interestingly, it submitted the applications for these two funds on Oct. 17, 2025. Therefore, these two funds had been awaiting launch for over 13 months.

As per the latest regulatory filings, Roundhill has been consistently delaying the effective dates for these two funds.

However, instead of launching them, the investment firm has decided to drop both products.

In its requests to withdraw the filings for these funds, Roundhill revealed that it "has no further intention to pursue effectiveness of the Fund." The firm noted that it had not sold any shares under the registrations for these two funds.

Intriguingly, Roundhill failed to elaborate on the sudden decision to axe its plans to launch these two ETFs.

Roundhill was planning to launch income-generating XRP and Solana ETFs using a covered call strategy. In such a strategy, investors sell options to earn premiums while also maintaining exposure to the price movements of XRP and Solana.

According to recent reports, unlike spot-based ETFs, these funds would not have held the cryptocurrencies directly. Instead, they would have used options written against existing cryptocurrency ETFs.

A covered call strategy can be useful for generating regular income. However, it can also cap profits during strong market rallies.

Notably, there has been relatively low demand for income-generating cryptocurrency investment products. This raises concerns about investors' interest in these ETFs.

Surprisingly, this decision came amid substantial net inflows into spot-based XRP and Solana ETFs.

In a recent development, U.S. spot XRP and Solana ETFs recorded net inflows of roughly $969 million between May and October 2026, according to data from SoSoValue.

Overall, these spot ETFs held around $3.26 billion in assets under management as of the end of October.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (961 w)

As cities act to shred housing’s red-tape, Boston homes in on parking

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that boston is an expensive place to build housing, and it is one of the priciest places in the country to live.
  • Industry observers note that cutting parking is one path cities are taking to lower construction costs.
  • Boulder, Colorado, set a 90-day deadline for deciding affordable housing applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that boston is an expensive place to build housing, and it is one of the priciest places in the country to live. Its City Council has taken a step toward scrapping one costly requirement: parking.

Industry observers note that cutting parking is one path cities are taking to lower construction costs. Others are chasing review time, density and tax incentives, and the changes are landing at the city and county level.

Boulder, Colorado, set a 90-day deadline for deciding affordable housing applications. Allentown, Pennsylvania, tied a tax break to affordable units. Lake County, Illinois, outside Chicago, opened all its residential zones to accessory dwelling units.

According to recent reports, these local moves come as states test how far they can push cities to build in the name of approving housing affordability. California, Texas and Florida have passed laws that override local zoning authority. Lawmakers there have had to keep tightening them to head off workarounds.

According to recent reports, illinois and North Carolina may be next. Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s housing reform initiative, which stalled this year, is expected to return in January.

Sources indicate that A shift in political winds in the Tar Heel State may mean lawmakers try once again to pass broad reform after failing multiple times. But they did eliminate off-street parking requirements across most of the state.

More than 120 cities have eliminated parking mandates, according to the Parking Reform Network, an advocacy coalition.

Industry observers note that boston could be next. The city’s average asking rent was $3,065 a month in the third quarter, the fifth highest of the 90 markets Cushman & Wakefield tracks, behind San Francisco, Latest York, San Jose and Long Island. Home construction fell by 14,000 units between 2024-2025 and 2025-2026, according to this year’s Greater Boston Housing Report Card.

The council voted 9-4 on Nov. 18 to remove parking requirements for newly introduced residential construction. The zoning commission must now approve the measure before it goes to the mayor.

Abundant Housing Massachusetts, the Commercial Real Estate Development Association, the Greater Boston Real Estate Board and the Environmental League of Massachusetts Action Fund support the measure.

Five years ago, Mayor Michelle Wu signed off on a zoning amendment to remove off-street parking requirements for affordable housing. Wu, who has championed zoning reform, hasn’t remarked whether she supports the current measure.

“We will evaluate the implications of eliminating parking minimums citywide,” spokesperson Marcela Dwork stated in a statement.

Boston’s transportation department indicates a garage space can cost up to $50,000, but the Pioneer Institute put underground spaces in Boston at $106,000 to $152,000 in late 2025.

Opponents argue the policy leaves out residents who need cars. But real estate professionals in Boston and elsewhere in the country note that such changes don’t mean parking vanishes.

In a recent development, “It’s about letting each Boston project respond to real demand, not one-size-fits-all formulas,” Reginald Jones-Booker, a Berkshire Hathaway agent, wrote on LinkedIn. “Developers can still include parking where it makes sense, but the mandate would no longer force every new home to meet a fixed minimum.”.

Boulder’s council unanimously approved an ordinance on Nov. 19 that sets a 90-day decision deadline for complete applications. It applies to projects in which at least half the homes are affordable to low- and middle-income households.

Site reviews there have taken a median of 277 days over the past two years, according to Boulder Reporting Lab. Staff, not the Planning Board, will decide requests for extra height or reduced open space, and neighbors can appeal.

The rules take effect Dec. 19. They are meant to keep Boulder eligible for Proposition 123, a 2022 voter-approved measure that sends state income tax revenue to affordable housing in cities that commit to growing their affordable stock by 3% a year.

Billy Joel’s 1982 hit “Allentown” made the Lehigh Valley city a symbol of a fading industrial America. Bethlehem Steel, the region’s anchor, ended most steelmaking in 1995 and was dissolved in 2003.

Those days are long gone, but the city now faces a different problem: keeping housing within reach as the region grows.

The City Council voted unanimously Nov. 18 to pass a workforce housing ordinance. Developers of projects with 10 or more units who receive a tax break under the Local Economic Revitalization Tax Assistance Act, a 1977 Pennsylvania law known as LERTA, must make at least 20% of the units affordable. Those units are rent-restricted for households earning 60% to 120% of area median income.

The city has no LERTA zone yet, so a council member mentioned the amended version “does not directly impact workforce housing today.”.

Lake County amended its Unified Development Ordinance on Nov. 10, effective that day, to allow accessory dwelling units in all county residential zones. It also lowers their minimum lot sizes, adds incentives for conservation developments and creates an “early assistance” process for developers. The rules reach only unincorporated areas.

The county acted while the state stalled. Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s Building Up Illinois Developments proposal, known as BUILD, would have legalized accessory dwelling units statewide, allowed missing-middle housing, set permit-review deadlines, ended excessive parking minimums and standardized impact fees.

It failed to advance before the spring session ended, after the Illinois Municipal League and suburban mayors objected to its zoning mandates. Pritzker has stated the plan will likely wait until January.

After Pritzker’s plan stalled, Illinois REALTORS revived its Illinois Housing Supply Accelerator Program, introduced in August. The program asks local officials to form working groups targeting barriers to building.

Pritzker mentioned in October that he expected BUILD to wait until the full session starting in January. Lawmakers finished the first week of the fall veto session without major housing action. They return Dec. 1-3.

Industry News: StepSecurity, led by two Microsoft vets, raises $20M to defend developers’ tools from hackers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.
  • Sources indicate that stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft.
  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

Sources indicate that stepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup announced a fresh round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

Sources indicate that stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The tech giant has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

“A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

Sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer remarked an investigation was underway.

That’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has said the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

It also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor mentioned up to 5,000 people may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

More than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company claims, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

According to recent reports, stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a company’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-new releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

It has been revealed that along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

It has been revealed that growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

In a recent development, the company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

According to recent reports, what’s next: StepSecurity intends to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The company indicates it also plans to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin led the daily ranking of stablecoin inflows into decentralized finance (DeFi), according to Token Terminal data that RWA Foundation shared on X.
