Recent findings suggest that paxos, Open Standard and Societe Generale followed with $7.8 million, $4 million and $1.2 million, respectively. World Liberty, United Stables, MetaMask, Tori and Liquity each added less than $700,000 over the same period.

In a recent development, about $2.8 billion worth of RLUSD is in circulation, compared with about $180 billion worth of Tether's USDT. Tether's stablecoin is still more than 60 times bigger than RLUSD.

It has been revealed that ripple launched RLUSD in December 2024. In mid-September 2026, RLUSD supply passed $2.44 billion, and about $1.38 billion of it was on Ethereum. About $1.05 billion was on the XRP Ledger, Ripple's home network. On Ethereum, the stablecoin is used in DeFi pools on Aave V3, Curve and Morpho.

Industry observers note that RLUSD is issued by Standard Custody & Trust under the supervision of the Latest York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS), and its reserves are held at custodian bank BNY. In the fall, RLUSD received a Moody's rating and was listed on Coinbase and Robinhood, and Ripple received final approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to launch Ripple National Trust Bank.

Ripple has also integrated RLUSD with payment providers Arf, Convera and Cross River Bank, and the stablecoin is now used in dollar settlements between companies.

In a CNBC interview on Nov. 19, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse called blockchain-based transactions "a wave of emerging technology." "I think 10 years from now you'll see blockchain implemented across our financial infrastructure," he stated.

Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different.
  • It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.
  • The firm mentioned today that users can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:36 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

The firm mentioned today that users can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

However, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant consumers first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

Anthropic mentioned people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the company said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s upcoming “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

It has been revealed that in a video posted on X, Anthropic revealed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq.

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026.

Sources indicate that because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to owners, Anthropic said.

It has been revealed that as an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic said. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

It has been revealed that there is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”.

That could be a pretty big downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

  • Lenders have spent years buying specialized tools for pricing, rate lock, hedging and loan due diligence.
  • The lender has promised a price on a loan that may take another month to fund, and the market can move during that window.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A borrower switches loan products after locking a rate. The lock desk updates the terms, but the hedge desk is still working from a file imported earlier that day. If the market moves before the next upgrade, the hedge desk is managing exposure against a pipeline that has already changed.

Lenders have spent years buying specialized tools for pricing, rate lock, hedging and loan due diligence. Each can do its job well while keeping a separate copy of the loan record. Rudy Zabran, chief operating officer at Consolidated Analytics, sums up the result as “five systems, five versions of the truth.” When terms change or an appraisal comes in, someone has to figure out which value is current and carry it into the next system.

A rate lock is also a hedge event. The lender has promised a price on a loan that may take another month to fund, and the market can move during that window. When the hedge desk relies on scheduled imports, it can learn about a lock or a change hours after the pricing engine and lock desk have recorded it. Extensions, relocks and float-downs can leave the desk estimating which loans will close based on an older view of the pipeline. If the mortgage hedging loan data still reflects the original product, the desk may need to revisit its coverage when the revised terms arrive.

Industry observers note that information must also flow back to pricing, too. Investor pay-ups, execution results and levels in the to-be-revealed mortgage-backed securities market can inform the next rate sheet. When those inputs sit apart from pricing, the secondary team has to bring them back into the process. By month-end, the team may still be tracing which version of the loan data drove a pricing or hedging decision.“The people who sit between the systems are rekeying data, re-importing tapes and deciding which number is the source of truth. The month-end P&L variance in secondary is usually a data variance in costume. Specialization is fine when volume pays for the overhead. As scale, you can afford a reconciliation team,” mentioned Zabran.

The cost of mortgage hedging errors and the work it takes to reconcile loan data rarely show up on a software invoice.

Together, those measures give lenders a baseline for judging whether a technology change makes day-to-day operations more efficient.

Sources indicate that A latest platform can leave manual work in place if one department still depends on a feature in the old system. Employees may still have to key changes into both systems, import another loan tape or recheck a field someone already verified. The work a lender can retire matters to the return on that investment.

Recent findings suggest that “What does this let me stop doing? Can I stop rekeying and stop reconciling and stop re-verifying data that we’ve already verified?” said Zabran.

After implementation, the same four measures can show which steps disappeared and where reconciliation still consumes staff time.

The discrepancies Consolidated Analytics sees in loan tapes offer a practical test for a vendor demo. Change the loan-to-value ratio on a sample loan, then compare the mortgage hedging loan data with the due diligence record to see when each reflects the revised figure. Ask the provider to follow the loan ID through pricing, lock, hedge, delivery and diligence and show whether the audit trail records the change. If the reports still disagree, trace how each module receives and stores the update.

The test should also cover access to the loan history. Can the lender retrieve it if a module goes offline? Which data and audit records can it take when it leaves a vendor? A specialist can still fit the workflow if it can read and update the shared loan record. That gives lenders room to keep a tool that serves a specific function without adding another copy of the data for staff to reconcile.

Consolidated Analytics built loanDNA around a question at the heart of its due diligence work. Can an investor trust the data on the loan? By the time an investor or rating agency asks, the lender may already have priced, locked and hedged the loan using figures that diligence will later flag. loanDNA maintains a shared loan record from rate lock through securitization, so teams can validate information earlier and preserve that work as the loan moves downstream.

In a recent development, the platform’s document intelligence tools extract data and classify documents, with human review supporting validation. The same engine handles pricing and rate lock, including for correspondent sellers. The hedge workflow reads the lock as an event, and standardized loan tapes carry data into investor delivery and diligence.

In a recent development, an appraisal illustrates what that can mean in practice. If the appraisal changes the loan-to-value ratio, the secondary team and diligence reviewers need to know which figure was used and when it changed. Carrying that history forward helps the lender explain why a figure in an earlier commitment differs from the one in the delivery tape. It also gives the lender a record to consult if an investor later asks how the loan was evaluated.

If volume doubled in 2027, how many people would a lender need to add in secondary and post-closing? The answer depends in part on how much work still falls between systems. When staff have to import tapes, reconcile lock changes and rebuild loan histories for investors, a surge in production can send more files into those same queues. Measuring that work now can show which handoffs would limit capacity first.

It has been revealed that consolidated Analytics looks to add live market feeds and execution capabilities to loanDNA. For lenders evaluating their systems today, the capacity test starts with the next change to a locked loan. How quickly does it reach the hedge desk, and how much work will it take to explain the change when the loan reaches an investor? The answers can show where a lender can absorb more volume and where growth will require more manual work.

#99134. Latest Update: How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1905 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • It has been revealed that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

It has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

It has been revealed that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

According to recent reports, the disastrous upgrade that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said Wednesday at the Latest York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella mentioned, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Industry observers note that some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Proposal) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

According to recent reports, MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a manufacturer partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

It has been revealed that since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the company with reports.

Industry observers note that the first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from fresh finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

In a recent development, moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

It has been revealed that no surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In a recent development, in theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple users to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

Recent findings suggest that more broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

According to recent reports, the cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to matter OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

Industry observers note that OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security matter involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

It has been revealed that think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

It has been revealed that managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

Industry observers note that it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

According to recent reports, it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solana has remained one of the major cryptocurrencies that have been heavily affected by the persistent crypto market volatility, stalling demand from both retail and institutional investors.

While Solana has continued to struggle amid the growing market uncertainty, it appears that traders are increasingly exiting their positions even across its DeFi market.

Recent data showcased by blockchain monitoring platform Lookonchain shows that two Solana whales unstaked a total of 2.31 million SOL on November 19.

While the total amount of SOL unstaked was worth about $169.4 million, further data demonstrated that the whales proceeded to transfer the tokens to Coinbase, a leading cryptocurrency exchange in the U.S.

It is important to note that the act of withdrawing SOL previously committed to the network's staking mechanism is regarded as unstaking.

While this move automatically gives holders the ability to transfer, sell, or use the unstaked tokens, the massive unstaking of 2.31 million SOL from large holders has drawn attention within the crypto community regarding the intention behind the move.

With curiosity on the rise about the whales' decision to move such a large amount of SOL to Coinbase Prime, the timing of the move has triggered speculation that the whales may be intending to sell the tokens.

Notably, the move arrived when Solana was trading around $74, briefly shifting into green territory just a few days after it retested $67, the lowest level seen since June 2026.

Since the prolonged price correction has continued to weaken investor confidence, it appears that the whales have acted upon the growing fear and withdrawn the assets they had initially committed to the Solana network to hedge against further losses.

Tech Report: Eight questions for evaluating PPE technology

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for mortgage lenders weighing whether to replace a core technology platform, the financial analysis can appear straightforward.
  • But those numbers tell only part of the story.
  • It has been revealed that consider a product, pricing and eligibility (PPE) engine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for mortgage lenders weighing whether to replace a core technology platform, the financial analysis can appear straightforward. Compare licensing fees, implementation expenses and ongoing operating costs, estimate the savings and calculate the return on investment.

But those numbers tell only part of the story. A less expensive platform may introduce operational limitations that offset the savings. Conversely, an investment that appears costly on paper may enable lenders to capture revenue opportunities, reduce recurring expenses or handle more business without adding staff.

It has been revealed that consider a product, pricing and eligibility (PPE) engine. When products, pricing rules, eligibility criteria and investor requirements are difficult to maintain, specialized staff spend more time testing changes, reconciling versions and correcting configuration issues. The same constraints can delay a newly introduced product’s path from strategy to production or introduce inconsistencies across channels, affecting both operating costs and revenue opportunities.

It has been revealed that scalability introduces another dimension. An engine that allows existing staff to support more loans, products, channels and pricing changes can give a lender room to respond to market cycles without rebuilding capacity each time conditions change. That flexibility has value beyond labor savings, allowing lenders to absorb growth, redirect specialized talent and protect service levels as volume changes.

Recent findings suggest that in part one of this series, we examined how pricing accuracy and execution quality affect the economics of PPE technology. Here, we put that analysis into practice with eight questions lenders can use to evaluate the full financial impact of their technology investments.

Industry observers note that none of these considerations automatically justifies replacing an existing engine. But they belong in the investment analysis alongside implementation expenses, licensing fees and other readily quantifiable costs.

A sound executive evaluation should compare one-time transition costs against recurring performance effects over a common decision horizon.

Here are eight questions to consider:.

Industry observers note that include implementation, integrations, data migration, internal labor, training and temporary disruption. Do not minimize these costs, but separate one-time items from recurring expenses.

Measure pricing errors, eligibility errors, rework, overrides, exception volumes and staff time devoted to correction and investigation.

Evaluate margin performance, pricing precision, responsiveness to volatility, pull-through, concession management and the consistency of pricing decisions.

Assess the volume that price administration, lock management, reporting and secondary marketing teams can support before requiring additional resources.

Measure feature-level utilization, not just platform availability. Realized value can change materially when adoption and transactional incidence are incorporated into the model.

It has been revealed that quantify the internal effort required to create, update, test, approve and monitor products, pricing rules, eligibility criteria and investor changes. Include duplicated configuration, regression testing, glitch remediation and dependence on scarce technical resources.

Measure the time from product approval to production availability, the effort required for validation and the consistency of pricing and eligibility across channels. Consider the revenue and competitive impact of delayed releases as well as the risk created by rushed or inaccurate configuration.

Identify revenue, margin, productivity or scalability improvements the organization cannot pursue effectively under the current operating model.

In a recent development, the resulting decision model should compare the net present value of transition costs with the ongoing financial and operational effects of each alternative. The objective is not to justify change in every case. It is to ensure that the decision accounts for the full economics of both changing and not changing.

Industry observers note that A complete PPE investment analysis should compare the full economics of changing technology with those of maintaining the status quo. That means measuring not only implementation expenses and licensing costs, but also recurring operational effects, execution quality and opportunities for growth. Only then can an executive team determine which investment offers the greatest long-term value.

This is the second part of a two-part series.

Sources indicate that jordan Brown is the founding principal and CEO of MarketWise Advisors, LLC, a management consulting firm focused on the mortgage and financial technology industries. Breaking: Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.
  • A fresh baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night?
  • But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

A fresh baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

Recent findings suggest that “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has problems with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla mentioned the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

In a recent development, birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on fresh parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

Recent findings suggest that that “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Industry observers note that turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our organization has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What do some of Hollywood's biggest blockbusters, Oscar-winning films and celebrated productions at the Cannes Film Festival have in common?
  • For more than a century, the German filmmaking technology company has helped shape how movies look and feel on screen.
  • Now imagine having some of that cinematic expertise in one's pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DUBAI, UAE, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What do some of Hollywood's biggest blockbusters, Oscar-winning films and celebrated productions at the Cannes Film Festival have in common? Beyond the famous faces and extraordinary storytelling, many share a connection to ARRI, a name one may never have heard of, but whose work one has almost certainly seen.

For more than a century, the German filmmaking technology company has helped shape how movies look and feel on screen. Its cameras have captured everything from spectacular action sequences to intimate moments that bring audiences closer to the characters they love.

Now imagine having some of that cinematic expertise in one's pocket.

Through its Cinematic Imaging Partnership with HONOR, ARRI is bringing selected elements of its professional filmmaking technology to smartphones. And with the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max arriving in the Middle East and Africa, that expertise is becoming accessible to a new generation of creators.

From a Small Munich Workshop to Hollywood.

Industry observers note that ARRI's story began in 1917, when two young film enthusiasts, August Arnold and Robert Richter, established a filmmaking equipment business in Munich, Germany. Combining their surnames to create ARRI, they began developing lighting equipment, film-processing machinery and other tools for the emerging motion picture industry.

Their ambitions soon extended to cameras. In 1924, ARRI developed its first camera, the KINARRI 35, followed by a breakthrough in 1937 with the ARRIFLEX 35. Its revolutionary mirror-reflex viewing system allowed filmmakers to see precisely what the camera was capturing, helping transform how films were shot.

Over the following decades, ARRI continued developing cameras and lighting technology that gave cinematographers greater freedom to bring their creative visions to life.

Industry observers note that then came another defining moment. In 2010, ARRI introduced its ALEXA digital camera system, which became widely recognised for its exceptional image quality, natural colours and ability to preserve detail in challenging lighting conditions.

According to recent reports, today, ARRI produces professional cameras, lenses, lighting systems and imaging technologies used across film and television productions worldwide. ARRI and its engineers have received 20 Scientific and Technical Awards from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

From the Oscars to Cannes: Behind Cinema's Biggest Moments.

It has been revealed that think of the sweeping desert landscapes, atmospheric scenes or breathtaking action sequences that define some of cinema's most memorable moments. Behind many of these experiences is ARRI technology, trusted by filmmakers to capture the visual details that bring stories to life.

Sources indicate that its influence continues today. At the 2026 Academy Awards, six of the ten Best Picture nominees were filmed using ARRI cameras. Guillermo del Toro's Frankenstein, captured entirely on the ARRI ALEXA 65, went on to win three Oscars.

At the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, ARRI cameras were used on 18 of the 22 films in the Main Competition, including Palme d'Or winner Fjord, which was captured with the ALEXA 35 and ARRI Master Anamorphic lenses.

But what makes ARRI so vital to filmmakers?

According to recent reports, beyond camera hardware, its expertise lies in how images reproduce light, colour, contrast and natural skin tones. Whether capturing an actor's expression in a dimly lit room or preserving the details of a sunset, ARRI's imaging technology helps filmmakers achieve the visual richness audiences associate with cinema.

And that expertise is now finding its way into smartphones.

Bringing Hollywood's Imaging Expertise to HONOR.

According to recent reports, think about the last time you recorded a beautiful sunset, only to discover that the sky looked washed out or someone's face disappeared into shadow. Or perhaps you filmed a special occasion, but the colours looked nothing like what you remembered.

These are among the challenges professional filmmakers have long worked to overcome.

At the heart of ARRI's expertise is ARRI Image Science, which determines how cameras interpret colour, lighting, highlights and shadows.

Through its collaboration with HONOR, selected elements of this technology are being adapted for mobile devices.

This is more than a branding partnership. HONOR contributes its mobile imaging hardware, AI capabilities and image-processing technologies, while ARRI brings its expertise in cinematic colour reproduction, image quality and professional filmmaking workflows.

Together, the companies are working to make sophisticated imaging techniques available in a device people carry every day.

Sources indicate that the collaboration also introduces professional features including ARRI LogC3, designed to retain more image information for editing, and ARRI Wide Gamut 3, which supports a broader range of colours. ARRI Looks allows creators to preview different cinematic styles while filming.

From Barcelona to One's Hands: The Partnership Journey.

The partnership was announced in March 2026 at Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, bringing together HONOR's mobile innovation and ARRI's century-long filmmaking heritage.

Its first commercial result arrived in August with the HONOR Robot Phone, then the collaboration reached another milestone in September with the launch of the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max in China.

Featuring ARRI branding on its camera module, the flagship introduced an end-to-end professional cinema workflow co-engineered with ARRI.

Its dual 200MP camera system, HONOR Imaging Chip H1 and 4K Cinematic LiveVideo capabilities work alongside ARRI Image Science to give creators greater control over how their footage is captured and finished.

This December, Hollywood Comes a Little Closer.

In a recent development, for years, smartphone cameras have competed on megapixels, zoom capabilities and AI-powered features. HONOR's collaboration with ARRI introduces another dimension: bringing the colour, atmosphere and creative control associated with professional cinema into mobile filmmaking.

With the HONOR Magic9 Pro Max making its Middle East and Africa debut, consumers will soon have an opportunity to experience that collaboration firsthand.

Sources indicate that the collaboration also reflects HONOR's evolving "Dare to Be" philosophy, which champions bold innovation, individuality and the confidence to challenge conventions. By bringing professional cinema technology into everyday devices, HONOR is encouraging a upcoming generation of creators to explore possibilities once reserved for professional filmmakers.

According to recent reports, leading cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase has announced the official listing of artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic (ANT) shares on its trading platform in the U.S. and U.K.

The listing comes as Anthropic, the company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude, officially made its much-anticipated stock market debut on Thursday, Nov. 19, with its shares seeing massive volatility.

Sources indicate that as per the latest X post from Coinbase, the exchange declared the availability of Anthropic (ANT) shares for eligible users in the U.S. and U.K.

Recent findings suggest that it's crucial to mention that ANT isn't a cryptocurrency but a traditional stock. Coinbase's support for ANT shares shows the company's efforts to expand its offerings beyond crypto into traditional financial markets.

Anthropic has set a new historic precedent, having successfully raised about $81 billion in its initial public offering (IPO). This is the biggest IPO ever.

The artificial intelligence tech giant sold 980 million shares at $83 per share, significantly higher than its previously unveiled price range of $70 to $78.

This brought Anthropic's initial valuation to about $1.5 trillion, making the company one of the most valuable publicly listed firms in the world right from the get-go.

But as Anthropic shares started trading on the Nasdaq exchange, the ANT ticker saw massive volatility.

As per Reuters, Anthropic shares began trading at $111.50. This represented an enormous 34% premium over the IPO price.

At the initial peak, Anthropic's market cap exceeded $2 trillion, surpassing SpaceX's valuation when it debuted on the market in June.

Anthropic shares slipped to around $95 as the stock gave back a significant chunk of its gains. This was partly due to investors looking to book their profits.

Nonetheless, Anthropic shares were still trading comfortably above their $83 IPO price.

The volatility surrounding Anthropic's stock market debut signals increasing doubts about the AI investment craze.

The listing of Anthropic shares is just one of Coinbase's moves to enter traditional financial markets.

Instead of just providing cryptocurrency trading, the exchange is looking to become a platform for multiple asset classes.

Interestingly, Coinbase had already listed Anthropic pre-IPO perpetual futures for eligible non-U.S. users on Nov. 18.

The perpetual futures were derivative contracts that allowed traders to speculate on Anthropic's valuation before its shares officially started trading on Nasdaq.

With the latest listing, eligible Coinbase users in the U.S. and U.K. can now trade the publicly listed Anthropic shares.

Anthropic's blockbuster debut comes as financial markets have been rocked by recent volatility, with tech stocks and crypto facing selling pressure.

#99125. On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (787 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

On a $1,000 Social Security check, Medicare’s 2027 premium hike eats 18% of the COLA raise—and hits small checks the hardest

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years.
  • Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first.
  • Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2027, Social Security recipients will get their biggest cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in four years. January’s benefits will be 3.6% higher, lifting the average retired worker’s monthly check to about $2,170, according to the Social Security Administration’s 2027 COLA announcement. The larger adjustment reflects persistent inflation in 2026.

Most COLA announcements fail to emphasize that Medicare takes its slice first. Starting in January, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced on Nov. 17 that the standard Part B premium rises by $6.50 to $209.40 a month. For most retirees, that premium is deducted straight from their Social Security benefit.

Although $6.50 doesn’t sound like much, it absorbs about 9% of the average retiree’s raise. And because the premium is a flat amount, the smaller the check, the bigger the share it takes.

It has been revealed that for a retiree collecting the 2026 average of $2,095 a month, the 3.6% COLA adds about $75. After the higher premium, roughly $69 remains, so Medicare claims about 9% of the increase.

Lower down the scale, the bite grows. A $1,000 monthly benefit rises by $36, but only $29.50 survives the premium hike, an 18% haircut on the raise. At $1,500 a month, the COLA is worth $54 and the net gain is $47.50, meaning 12% of the raise goes to Medicare.

Sources indicate that bigger checks barely feel it. A $2,500 benefit gains $90 and keeps $83.50, losing 7% of the increase. At $3,000 a month, the raise is $108, the net gain is $101.50, and the premium takes just 6%.

That math applies to retirees who pay the standard premium out of their benefits. Higher-income enrollees pay income-based surcharges on top of it, while states cover the Part B premium for about one in five Medicare enrollees with low incomes and savings.

In a recent development, by recent standards, this year’s hike is mild. The 3.2% premium increase is smaller than the COLA for the first time since 2023; in 2026, the premium jumped 9.7% against a 2.8% COLA.

Even though COLAs are treated like bonuses or raises, they’re not. As David Herbert, director of economics & economic freedom and a senior research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research (AIER), told The Hill, “It’s meant to make sure that Social Security recipients are receiving the same amount of spending power as they did in the past. It’s not actually going to make them wealthier or have an easier time buying things that they weren’t already going to buy.”.

Industry observers note that seniors appear to agree. In an AARP survey conducted before the announcement, 80% of Social Security recipients said a projected 3.5% COLA in 2027 would not keep up with rising prices. When the final number landed, some retirees dismissed it as too little to offset soaring costs.

In a recent development, it seems as though seniors are right. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 3.7% annual inflation for September 2026, its most recent annual figure. The 3.6% COLA will not keep up, especially since the higher payments don’t start until January.

In a recent development, by then, seniors will have absorbed higher prices since March, when inflation hit 3.3% and outpaced the 2026 COLA of 2.8%. It peaked at 4.2% in May. In other words, a 3.6% COLA is a small improvement, but it comes too late.

Against the backdrop of higher benefits and costs looms Social Security’s insolvency. The 2026 Trustees Report found that starting in the fourth quarter of 2032, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund will no longer be able to pay 100% of scheduled benefits. Instead, recipients would receive only 78% of them.

Recent findings suggest that part of the funding shortfall comes down to demographics. According to the trustees’ projections, about 2.6 workers paid in for every beneficiary in 2025, compared with 41.9 in 1945. The trustees expect the ratio to keep falling, to about 1.9 workers per beneficiary by 2075.

With fewer workers paying into Social Security, “Congress is going to have to step in and do something,” said Herbert. “What is going to be left over for people who are not quite at retirement but are hoping at some point to see any form of a return on investment on this money that we’ve been sending the federal government for our entire working lives?”.

Sources indicate that that job falls to the new Congress, which convenes in January and has roughly six years to act before automatic cuts kick in. In the meantime, Herbert advises those a decade or two from retirement to start saving and investing. More importantly, workers shouldn’t initiative on receiving full Social Security benefits in retirement.

#99124. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1450 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video manufacturer everyone used during the pandemic.
  • Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters.
  • The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the manufacturer outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 23:43 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video manufacturer everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and declared its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the manufacturer outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

Industry observers note that the concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

Nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Industry observers note that zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”.

Industry observers note that AI agents are rapidly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually remarked to one another and to customers.

It has been revealed that “Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan mentioned. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

In a recent development, my Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan said it is nearing 2 million monthly active people, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

According to recent reports, that is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

Sources indicate that A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Industry observers note that customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang stated.

According to recent reports, customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom noted at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers fresh to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

According to recent reports, chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she remarked, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a major winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

According to recent reports, there is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan said. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another manufacturer’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

In a recent development, some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a firm that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these challenges came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”.

According to recent reports, zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the tech giant is in transition, so it’s key to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

Sources indicate that for information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

That is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

Microsoft ‘To Do’ people make a significant to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm.
  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal people that Microsoft To Do would be their newly introduced home.
  • According to recent reports, microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:08 pm.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal people that Microsoft To Do would be their newly introduced home. Now it’s asking them to switch again.

According to recent reports, microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the organization’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

Sources indicate that that’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Industry observers note that why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A fresh Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday people, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft declared Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Recent findings suggest that rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

According to recent reports, the most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and remarked it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the organization in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist people may end up back with the people who built it.

‘This seems like an extreme privacy violation.’ Surprising messages from the Muse AI agent are unnerving Meta’s own employees, report says

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meta employees have raised concerns about the firm’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters.
  • In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.
  • It has been revealed that “This seems like an extreme privacy violation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meta employees have raised concerns about the firm’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters.

In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.

It has been revealed that “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee posted.

A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported.

Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse remarked, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”.

Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.”.

In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating, owing to built-in prompts that were designed to engage consumers between sessions, according to Reuters.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that other cases involved “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.”.

The random, out-of-context messages were confirmed as hallucinations.

A Meta spokesperson noted employee testing is core to product development and is meant to generate feedback in order to implement privacy safeguards, adding that employees have access to versions of Muse that are different from those the public has and that some functions aren’t available elsewhere.

As for the Muse messages that referred to encrypted Signal chats, the spokesperson pointed out that Android consumers have the option to grant apps notification access, which they must opt in to and is not specific to Muse.

“With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on,” Meta explained.

Recent findings suggest that since Muse was launched in September, it’s been downloaded more than 10 million times, becoming one of the fastest-growing apps ever. It’s also key to the social media giant’s blueprint to generate billions of dollars in revenue from AI.

In a recent development, but other companies are blocking Muse and other AI agents. For example, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon remarked the bank won’t allow agents to access customer accounts and act on their behalf.

Similarly, Amazon won’t let Muse shop on its e-commerce platform and is already fighting to keep out Perplexity’s AI agents.

The process of raising those barriers, however, also entails network upgrades that may be contributing to a sudden surge in outages.

In recent weeks, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, Apple, and Microsoft saw temporary service disruptions. U.S. officials have said there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting software patches were deployed before all the bugs were worked out.

Industry observers note that because AI tools can find vulnerabilities faster than companies can safely fix them, the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed, Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times.

In an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent firm Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.

“This is a significant blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he remarked. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”.

#99119. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1017 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the manufacturer acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company claims it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

Industry observers note that what set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software enhancement that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows upgrade used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

According to recent reports, the final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report states.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Sources indicate that second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Recent findings suggest that third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report notes.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate matter.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

It has been revealed that once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft claims it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft states it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It has been revealed that it also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

According to recent reports, microsoft states its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it intends to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft mentioned the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the firm says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.
