📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to defense tech, it’s a FOMO-YOLO market, two prominent investors in the sector mentioned onstage this week at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit.

“I’m a long-term optimist, and I’ve been doing this for 30 years, but I see activity in the capital markets that reminds me of 2021,” mentioned Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners.

“There are a lot of new entrants into the space. The death of SaaS and the disruption from AI has shifted capital into areas of deep tech, space, robotics, energy, and defense,” he noted. “There’s folks deploying capital who aren’t experts in any one of those sectors. So, consequently, we can talk about a bubble.”.

In a recent development, the money has arrived fast. Venture capitalists put a record $37.9 billion into defense tech across 269 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 117.5% from the prior quarter, according to PitchBook data cited by Fortune in its coverage of defense tech CEOs at the forum. Valuations have climbed with it: Early-stage defense startups have fetched 17 to 50 times revenue, Fortune reported this summer.

According to recent reports, even the sector’s biggest winners are uneasy. Anduril cofounder Trae Stephens told Fortune in June that mid-stage defense startups trade at multiples that are “completely disconnected from reality.”.

Aidan Madigan-Curtis, a partner at venture firm Eclipse, described the mood bluntly.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a pretty significant YOLO sentiment happening right now, essentially in physical tech investing,” Madigan-Curtis noted. “There are a lot of tourist investors who are excited about a person, a background, a theme … [and] maybe they’re most excited about who invested in the last round and the signal that that gives, versus a hardcore underwriting of a real set of capabilities that can truly pierce into a market.”.

That froth now meets a broader shock. Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12, under pressure from the chipmaker’s board, has left the startup ecosystem primed for change and possible disruption.

AI startups are most exposed, but private capital markets more broadly are in flux, including the deep-tech bets now crowding into defense.

Industry observers note that for startups, the harder test is selling to the government. It has long been a difficult market to crack, and the Pentagon, which has used the name Department of War as a secondary title since a 2025 executive order, is among the hardest. Part of the trouble is that government isn’t a monolithic customer, even if it looks like one.

“There’s a misconception that the Pentagon is this all-or-nothing type of customer,” said Faltas. “It’s actually not. The building itself is … called the Pentagon. It’s got five corners, and each of those five corners needs to be engaged with, and educated with, and listened to … That requires a very focused ground game.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, formal verification startup Sequent Inc.
  • Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set.
  • Industry observers note that curve also figures in how Sequent got started.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 02:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

In a recent development, formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today confirmed that it has raised $2.2 million in fresh funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Industry observers note that curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

According to recent reports, following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who stated AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

According to recent reports, for now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

In a recent development, for two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor intends priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Industry observers note that frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”.

The trader's latest post on X highlights a pattern he has found throughout Bitcoin's price history: previous bull runs have always ended with devastating market corrections.

"Every bull market phase in the history of BTC has ended with at least a 75% correction of the prior parabolic bull trend," Brandt's X post reads.

Continuing his warning, Brandt raised an alarming question: "Is this what is happening with Bitcoin?".

In a recent development, the trading veteran has not put a number on the possible crash. But his words point toward the possibility that the current drop in Bitcoin might be part of a larger correction and not just a temporary dip.

A look at Bitcoin's historical crashes could paint a scary picture.

Bitcoin has a history of sharp corrections following major bull runs.

For example, the crypto asset dropped by around 84% from its December 2017 high to its December 2018 low. Another example of such a deep price correction can be found in the 2022 bear market, when BTC saw a drop of around 77% from its November 2021 all-time high.

These historic crashes have shown the extreme losses that Bitcoin investors have faced during such market corrections.

It has been revealed that at the time of writing on Nov. 20, Bitcoin is right now trading at around $62,000, which is almost 51% below its October 2025 all-time high.

If it were to undergo a 75% price correction from its all-time high, then it would drop to around $31,550.

But it's worth mentioning that Brandt referred to a correction of the prior parabolic bull trend, which may not be the same as a 75% correction from the peak.

Interestingly enough, this is not the first time the trader has warned about an even darker future for Bitcoin's price.

LONDON, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Clarivate Plc (NYSE: CLVT), a leading global provider of transformative intelligence, today announced that leading global corporations and IP law firms, including Mercari, Brndpwr and Sterne Kessler, are development partners for IPOne, an AI-native platform which connects across patents, trademarks and litigation intelligence.

IPOne is being developed to bring together Clarivate trusted, curated IP data with specialized AI capabilities to power IP research and workflows. Customers will be able to use IPOne directly, or integrate Clarivate intelligence into enterprise AI environments, including Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft Copilot and OpenAI's ChatGPT. It is being developed in close collaboration with corporate IP teams and leading law firms to ensure its capabilities across research, analysis, monitoring and decision support are shaped around the real-world workflows, challenges and decisions of IP professionals.

Recent findings suggest that simon Webster, President, Intellectual Property, Clarivate, said: "The future of IP intelligence will be shaped by bringing trusted data, advanced technology and human expertise together in the environments where professionals work. By developing IPOne alongside leading corporate IP teams and law firms, we are grounding our innovation in the real decisions and workflows our customers navigate every day.

"Our partners' expertise helps us build technology that is practical, responsible and designed to deliver meaningful value across the IP lifecycle.".

Alongside Mercari, Brndpwr and Sterne Kessler, IPOne's development partners include some of the world's largest energy, beauty, beverage and consumer goods companies, from the U.S. and Europe to the Middle East, as well as an Am Law 100 law firm.

Sources indicate that hidekazu KAMINO, Intellectual Property Patent Attorney, Mercari, said: "As AI becomes increasingly embedded in intellectual property workflows, it is important that latest technology is shaped by the professionals who will use it. Working with Clarivate on IPOne has shown us how trusted IP intelligence and AI can help improve the detection of potential trademark infringement and enable teams to respond more promptly and effectively.".

According to recent reports, job van Mierlo, Founder, Brndpwr, said: "The value of AI in intellectual property depends on the quality of the intelligence behind it and how effectively it supports day-to-day decision-making. Working with Clarivate through the IPOne development partner program gives us the opportunity to help shape solutions that bring trusted data and AI together around the real challenges facing IP teams.".

Robert Burger, Chief Operating Officer and Executive Director, Sterne Kessler, said: "As a development partner for IPOne, we are bringing the perspective of practicing attorneys to the creation of an intelligence platform designed specifically for IP. We believe this collaboration will help build a stronger foundation for how professionals access, interpret and apply IP intelligence, supporting more informed decisions throughout the innovation lifecycle.".

It has been revealed that IPOne is designed to extend trusted Clarivate intelligence into the tools and environments where IP professionals increasingly work; this includes Derwent patent data, Darts-ip litigation intelligence and CompuMark trademark and industrial design data. Whether used directly or accessed through the enterprise AI tools customers already use, secure integrations including MCP and API access are designed to enable organizations to embed IP intelligence into their AI environments and workflows while maintaining transparency and control.

‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled.
  • The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov.
  • In a recent development, on Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the firm at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

In a recent development, on Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

In a recent development, techCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares, and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

It has been revealed that the largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the manufacturer unveiled in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

Industry observers note that the fund can grow. Anthropic claims its board may add another 2% of the manufacturer for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company noted it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not announced a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the organization matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to plan documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

That money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

In a recent development, the third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts, and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

It has been revealed that the cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

Some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter, and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a manufacturer spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

It has been revealed that anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

Separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic states it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

Sources indicate that the next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the company’s matches can start to move.

Sources indicate that until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

XRP price is still struggling to get back above $1, even after the Nvidia-led market bounce that happened to be just a temporary day. Now, the XRP Ledger has another headline, with developers preparing to wipe its Testnet and Devnet tomorrow following an infrastructure failure.

Sources indicate that the reset is scheduled for November 25, between 5 and 6 PM Pacific time. Everything sitting on the two networks goes. Accounts, balances, transactions, AMMs, escrows, offers, and other ledger data will be cleared. With this going on, developers are forced to rebuild their testing environments.

In a recent development, XRP, meanwhile, couldn’t make much of Monday’s rebound. Ripple briefly reclaimed $1 before being pushed back down in a dead cat bounce situation.

An XRPL Testnet reset and the upgrade to XRPL 3.5 are coming up 🚨​Here’s what it actually means, what happens to the data, why traders look at past BTC/XRP price action, and what the upcoming institutional features bring Why the reset & what gets wiped?Ripple flagged an concern in… pic.twitter.com/xhvrjtjWDs.

It has been revealed that the reset is not a routine wipe, so XRPL’s Testnet depended on a single full-history server that crashed and could not be recovered. Ripple states it is increasing storage capacity to address the problem and reduce how frequently the network needs resetting.

Developers will lose their existing setups and need to collect fresh test XRP from the faucet. Those running their own servers will also need to clear their databases and restart them after the reset.

Testnet is used to mirror Mainnet’s amendment status, while Devnet gives developers a place to experiment with proposed features. Both serve as sandboxes, meaning the reset won’t touch real XRP or live ledger activity.

A clean testing environment matters when teams are building upcoming applications, experimenting with features, or checking integrations before they reach the live network. Losing existing test data is inconvenient, but keeping a broken full-history server running isn’t much of an option either.

Ripple states the network URLs, IDs, and validator settings will remain unchanged. Developers can reuse some addresses, but recreated AMM pools will generally have different account addresses.

#99108. Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

Etzioni on AI: The outage conspiracy theories are wrong — our rush to patch and upgrade is the culprit

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.
  • In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down.
  • Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 22, 2026 at 7:04 amNovember 22, 2026 at 7:06 am.

In less than a week, Microsoft email went dark around the world, the FAA halted every departure in the country, Chase payments stalled, Apple’s services faltered and the NSA’s internal network went down. Sen. Josh Hawley remarked that if this was all a coincidence, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Yet intelligence and law enforcement officials told Congress they’ve found no evidence that anyone was attacking us.

Attackers typically announce when they’ve hit you. Terrorists claim credit. Criminals concern ransom notes and often brag as well: the hackers who crippled MGM’s casino systems in 2023 told TechCrunch within days. None of this month’s outages came with any of that.

Sources indicate that could a state actor be flexing its cyber capabilities to warn us? China’s Volt Typhoon hackers kept access to U.S. critical infrastructure for at least five years before anyone made it public, positioning themselves to disrupt it in a future crisis. However, hackers who are that patient don’t blow their cover by knocking out the world’s email. A warning shot also works only if the target knows who fired it, and we don’t have a credible suspect for a shooter here.

Sources indicate that each outage has a separate origin tracing back to the organization’s own systems: a newly introduced router a contractor was installing for the FAA, a bug Microsoft shipped in July, a software bug at Chase, an internal update at Apple, a patch at the NSA. To stage that, a single attacker would have to break into three companies and two federal agencies, disguise every intrusion as a routine mistake and leave nothing for investigators to find.

Sources indicate that A far more credible root cause is the patch treadmill set at too high a speed: AI is finding security holes faster than anyone can safely fix them, and the rush to patch and upgrade is making everything more fragile. Think of an immune system in overdrive. It fights off infection, and sometimes it attacks healthy tissue. This month’s outages were a flare-up.

In a recent development, on Nov. 17, the startup Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java, the software platform used by government agencies and about 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Calif found it with OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model. Oracle shipped a patch the same day, and a federal alert urged organizations to “immediately patch.”.

Industry observers note that last month the same startup used OpenAI models to find a flaw in PHP, the programming language behind an estimated 70% of websites, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton tied the NSA’s outage to the patching that followed. Microsoft alone fixed 1,413 vulnerabilities in October, more than its previous record for an entire year.

Recent findings suggest that AI is forcing faster fixes. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella states his organization’s outage came from a dormant bug, but he warned this week that AI-driven patching could bring more instability. AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” he told CNBC.

A patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week, he said at the New York Times DealBook Summit. Now it “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that criminals and state-backed hackers are already using ARTEX, an open-source AI tool built for testing a company’s own defenses, with some intrusions going from first targeting to administrator-level access in under three hours. So the patching can’t slow down. Nobody would give up their immune system to avoid a flare-up.

It has been revealed that it will get worse before it gets better. Calif’s CEO, Thai Duong, expects Java4Shell to threaten systems that don’t upgrade for the next five to 10 years.

Meanwhile, the AI that finds flaws like this one is spreading. Open-weight models, which anyone can download and run without safeguards, trail the most advanced models on cyber tasks by only four to seven months, according to the UK AI Security Institute. Every month will bring more bugs, more emergency patches and more flare-ups.

It has been revealed that there’s a finite amount of code in Windows, iOS and Chrome, and every bug AI finds and fixes there is one an attacker can’t use. Partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, a program to secure critical software before AI can be turned against it, found more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity bugs in its first month.

Former Microsoft security staffer Angela Gunn sees a hopeful sign: more and more unrelated researchers are turning up the same bugs, which suggests the supply is finite. Fixing still lags finding, but the giants have the money and people to catch up. Within a year or two, I expect Windows, iOS and Chrome to be more secure than they’ve ever been.

AMSTERDAM and LONDON, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (Cboe: CBOE), a leading global markets operator and pioneer in equity and index derivatives, today declared that Cboe Clear Europe, its pan-European central counterparty (CCP), has cleared more than 1.5 billion client equity trades so far in 2026, eclipsing its previous annual record of 1.49 billion in 2022. The milestone reflects continued client adoption of Cboe Clear Europe's services, reinforcing its position as a leading pan-European cash equities CCP and underscoring growing demand for competitive, open-access clearing.

Vikesh Patel, Global Head of Clearing and President, Cboe Clear Europe, said: "Surpassing our previous annual record at this point in the year demonstrates the trust market participants place in Cboe Clear Europe and the value of the efficiencies we offer. Because we compete for every trade we clear, this represents participants actively choosing us for our cost effectiveness, risk management capabilities and capital and operational efficiencies, as well as their confidence in the benefits of the open-access clearing model for European equities.".

Recent findings suggest that cboe Clear Europe's open-access approach allows participants to consolidate their cash equities clearing at a single CCP regardless of where they trade, unlocking significant netting efficiencies and lower settlement costs. During 2026, Cboe Clear Europe's cash equity network expanded to 56 venues and market segments, the broadest coverage of any European CCP. Cboe Clear Europe supports two primary venue connection models: interoperability, which gives participants full choice of CCP; and preferred clearing, where trades are cleared at a participant's chosen CCP when selected by both counterparties to a trade.

Key market share1 milestones in 2026 include:.

Cboe Clear Europe has also been at the forefront of industry efforts to expand competition in European equities clearing through the EU's Market Integration and Supervision Package (MISP). The firm co-signed an industry letter alongside leading buy-side and sell-side trade associations calling for mandatory interoperability among, at a minimum, significant CCPs for equities as part of MISP (full letter here).

Patel added: "Europe is at a decisive point in turning its ambition for more competitive, efficient and integrated capital markets into reality. Our volumes demonstrate that participants want choice in clearing, and now is the time to embed that competition across the market. Mandating clearing interoperability across all major equities CCPs would let firms consolidate their clearing where it is most efficient for them and help deliver the regulatory objective of more integrated European capital markets.".

Alongside cash equities, Cboe Clear Europe has continued to expand its securities financing transactions (SFTs) service, which has introduced central clearing to a market that has historically operated bilaterally. Released in 2025 for loans of European equities and ETFs, the service was extended this year to fixed income and US equities lendable assets, delivering the benefits of central clearing across the global securities lending market. It reached a record â¬20 billion in outstanding loan value in September 2026.

Industry News: Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any organization planning to concern under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

It has been revealed that the OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

In a recent development, the OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

Industry observers note that the Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

Recent findings suggest that the main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

It has been revealed that on diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board claims it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Sources indicate that redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

It has been revealed that the Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

It has been revealed that concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

Latest Update: Women’s soccer has a $1 billion opportunity—and the CEO of England’s top two leagues wants a slice of the pie

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for women’s football, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers.
  • Industry observers note that since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly.
  • Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the company responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the 1999 FIFA Women’s World Cup final was a watershed moment for women’s football, with record-breaking attendance and viewership numbers. More than 40 million people in North America tuned in to watch the U.S. beat China 5–4 on penalties in the final. Among them was ­ Canadian Nikki Doucet, then a student and college basketball player at St. Francis Xavier University. “That was the first time I’d seen women’s team sports on TV, and I remember feeling so excited,” she says.

Industry observers note that since then, interest in women’s football has grown significantly. Its global fan base is projected to surpass 800 million by 2030, according to Nielsen Sports, while Fifpro expects the sport to be a $1 billion industry by 2027—a 72% increase from 2024.

Now CEO of Women’s Super League Football, the company responsible for operating the top two English women’s leagues (WSL and WSL2), Doucet is at the sharp end of that opportunity. England has become a commercial force in women’s football: Eight of the world’s 15 highest-revenue clubs are in the WSL, according to Deloitte, and Doucet believes the league is well-positioned to capture a “significant portion” of the potential $1 billion the sport is predicted to generate.

Sources indicate that american entrepreneurs and investment groups are taking note. The success of the Women’s National Basketball Association—now an $850 million franchise—and the soaring valuations of teams in the National Women’s Soccer League (league leaders Gotham FC were recently valued at $350 million) underlines the potential. And many see an opportunity to buy in at an early stage in the commercial development of the sport in Europe.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.U.S. businesswoman Michele Kang bought the London City Lionesses in 2023, leading the club to its 2025 WSL promotion. Other notable investors include Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who holds a minority stake in Chelsea FC Women, and U.S. financier Marc Zahr, an investor in Aston Villa Women.

Speaking at the WSL’s New Playbook ­ summit earlier this year, one investor argued that European women’s football represented the “best opportunity in sport,” on a risk-adjusted basis.

“I think of my career as if I’m still an athlete. I practice for every board meeting in the same way that I used to train for a game. Your practice should be so hard, the game is easy.”.

Industry observers note that “The enterprise value of these clubs is 100% going up,” Doucet, a former investment banker at Citi, notes. “The question is, do you have owners that want to participate in this asset class of women’s football? There are different tradeoffs versus men’s football and different risk factors because we’re in a different stage of development.”.

In a recent development, doucet’s challenge is turning rising global interest in the women’s game into regular paying customers. There was a surge in interest following the England Lionesses’ UEFA Women’s Euro 2022 victory: Average attendance at WSL matches tripled to 5,616 the following season. But last year, median attendance was 3,236—and it remains heavily concentrated in a few clubs.

“This isn’t a manufacturing challenge. This is a marketing and revenue challenge,” Doucet claims. The league invested in a rebrand of both the WSL and WSL2 ahead of the newly expanded league this season, and clubs are also investing more. In April, WSL team Brighton declared prepares to build Europe’s first purpose- built women’s football stadium at an estimated cost of more than £75 million ($99 million).

“You have to invest in building the foundations that will generate long- term returns, but they might take time until you actually see the results,” Doucet claims. “That’s the constant tradeoff.”.

It has been revealed that the underlying economics also remain fragile. Despite the high revenues, only four of the 14 clubs in the WSL recorded a profit (two clubs did not publish detailed financial data). The league itself, which is co-owned by the participating clubs, posted an operating loss of £8.2 million ($10.8 million) for the year ending July 2025.

In a recent development, doucet attributes much of the loss to one-off costs associated with becoming an independent business, including establishing its own HR, finance, legal, and regulatory teams. The WSL and WSL2 formally split from the Football Association (FA) in 2024, shortly after Doucet joined the organization. She says the league is now profitable, although declined to share the financial details.

“We’re in a transition phase, which is probably a little bit messy. The challenge is going from big structural moments, like a World Cup, to building a weekly fan habit around women’s professional football,” Doucet states.

Sources indicate that the majority of the league’s revenues so far have come from broadcast rights and commercial partnerships. The league generated £8.7 million ($11.5 million) from Sky and the BBC in 2025, and the league counts Doucet’s former employer Nike, in addition to Airbnb, Apple, and ­ Barclays, among its growing list of sponsors.

In a recent development, the opportunities for commercial sponsors are different from those in the men’s sport, Doucet says. “We have a different audience that really values companies that are investing in women’s football,” she says. “They’re very brand loyal, and they show much deeper engagement.”.

Doucet’s current priority is improving the spectacle on the pitch. “The fans want to watch the best players, and they want to watch a competition that’s exciting and has jeopardy,” she states. Good progress has been made in this area, too. The London City Lionesses signed three-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas from Barcelona this summer, and the WSL had the highest representation of players at last year’s Women’s Euro tournament of any league.

Ensuring the WSL’s longevity is a responsibility Doucet is acutely aware of. “This isn’t a five-year business,” she indicates. “This is a generational asset.” She remains optimistic about what lies ahead. Doucet adds: “We’re in an early stage, so the potential is almost completely untapped—you don’t know how big it could be.”.

This article appears in the December 2026/January 2027 issue of Fortune with the headline “Women’s football has a $1 billion opportunity—and the WSL wants a slice of the pie.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most people who see something odd on Instagram mutter “huh, neat,” and keep scrolling. Michael Ramsey bought a plane ticket to check it out in person. The former oil and gas marketer, who once ran an F45 studio in Port Melbourne, saw a post about an exercise machine called the Rowformer, and flew from Australia to Orange County to try it himself. Seven years later, STRONG Pilates has more than 130 studios across multiple countries and continents, 57,000 members and more than $75 million in net revenue over the past 12 months.

Ramsey shared how the STRONG brand came together, why some Pilates traditionalists hate it, and why he is totally okay with that.

It has been revealed that this wasn’t your original career path. How did you get involved in Pilates?I was working in oil and gas, and I was not enjoying my life too much. I wasn’t highly motivated in corporate. And on the weekends, I was actually running a nightclub with my business partner, Mark Armstrong, who I’ve been in business with for eleven years. And he tapped me on the shoulder and he said, “Hey, I found this really unique boutique concept called F45 Training.” This was about twelve years ago. And so we actually brought the first F45 studio to Melbourne, Australia, and I quit my job in corporate, and for the first time in my life, I felt free, like I was in charge of my own destiny. Not only did I have financial freedom, but I had time as well. We scaled our F45 studios to six very quickly, sold after about four or five years.

Industry observers note that what inspired STRONG?My housemate indicated me an Instagram post about this Rowformer machine that was created out of Orange County. And to me it ticked a lot of boxes — you’ve got rowing, and you’ve got the Reformer. So I jumped on a plane, took the class and it was one of the most exhilarating, endorphin-led kind of workouts I’d ever done. I’m looking around the room, and there are all these incredibly fit women in their forties and fifties that just looked incredible. And I’m like, “Wow, this, this is awesome. I need to take this back to Australia.” Mark tried it, had the same experience, and then we negotiated global rights for the machine and built a franchise model around it.

Most of us see something cool on Instagram and keep scrolling. We don’t jump on a plane. What does that say about you?Look, to be transparent, it was very opportunistic. I could see, and nothing against F45, but I couldn’t see the lifetime value of the customer increasing over time due to the impact of workouts. So I was on the hunt for something that was low impact, more longevity-focused. How do we keep our members for five, six, seven, ten years? That was a question that I had and the problem I was trying to solve.

How do you turn early adopters into paying clients and repeat customers?You need to respect your product and business enough to have people paying from the start. There’s this whole thing in the fitness industry about free trials, and do they work or do they not work? We are a premium product, and I think once the work is done and the product is ready, you need to respect yourself and your product by charging for every session.

Now, for anyone who’s starting in this space, I would say the first thing to do is just start. Just open, and then learn from your consumer and innovate like crazy. And that’s all we did. It’s a very different product today than what it was seven years ago, and in another seven years it’s gonna be probably even more different, because that’s how it works. If you don’t innovate, you will recede, and you will die.

According to recent reports, was there an innovation that came from customer feedback and made you think, “Oh yeah, that’s a good idea”?The big one was the TV screens. Our male audience, as soon as we put TVs in, their trial-to-member conversion went through the roof. You’ve got to imagine, seven years ago, a lot of men hadn’t even experienced Pilates before. They were terrified to jump on a reformer. So the TVs, although they’re not liked by the traditionalists, gave us a huge uptake, particularly with male consumers. It was huge for us.

Your Instagram handle is just “Strong.” How on earth did you get that?Do you remember when domain names were getting really expensive? Like imagine strong.com. It’s probably worth half a million dollars. I had some friends that were trying to open businesses and trying to get these domain names, and I thought, “Well, I’m gonna start acquiring one-word Instagram names,” because Instagram was really taking off at the time. And so I had Strong, I had Cultivate, I had Ram. So I just held onto them. And then when I went to Orange County and I did the workout, I thought, “How does this workout make me feel? Not only do I need to be physically strong, but I need to be mentally strong to get through this.” And so it just made sense to call it STRONG Pilates, and now we’re here. At one point, it was getting tagged every 30 seconds all around the world, and I would just sit there watching it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WARSAW, Poland, Nov. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Global non-bank business lender Bizcap has officially launched operations in Poland, marking another significant milestone in its European expansion and bringing its fast, flexible funding solutions to the country's small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

The launch follows Bizcap's entry into Luxembourg in July 2025 and subsequent expansion into Germany in October 2025, strengthening its growing presence across Europe.

Having unveiled plans to explore Poland as a potential market earlier this year, Bizcap has since identified strong opportunities to support local businesses seeking alternatives to traditional bank finance.

With a dynamic SME sector and growing demand for accessible business funding, Poland represents an attractive market for Bizcap's established non-bank funding model, which prioritises speed, flexibility and a broader approach to assessing business funding applications.

Sources indicate that leading Bizcap's Polish operations is Managing Partner Oskar Kowalski, who brings more than 15 years of experience across investment banking, private equity, venture capital and alternative finance. He is also a founding member of Bizcap's US operations.

Originally from Poland, Kowalski spent much of his life in the United States before returning to his home country to lead Bizcap's local market expansion.

Recent findings suggest that "Poland has a dynamic and ambitious SME sector, with thousands of entrepreneurs driving innovation, creating jobs and contributing to economic growth. Yet accessing business funding through traditional channels can still be challenging," Kowalski mentioned.

"We see a tremendous opportunity to introduce a faster, more flexible financing alternative that better reflects how modern businesses operate.".

Kowalski mentioned the official launch follows months of market exploration, planning and preparation to establish Bizcap's local operations.

In a recent development, "We've spent the past several months understanding the local funding landscape and building a strong team. We're now ready to put that work into action and support Polish businesses with funding solutions that have already proven successful internationally," he remarked.

According to recent reports, kowalski is joined by Anna Kozlowska, who has been appointed Chief Operating Officer of Bizcap Poland, who has extensive experience in financial services and fintech operations. Kozlowska brings 12 years of experience in fintech and innovation, having led sales, business development and operations. She previously served as CEO of SME lender Finiata.

"Having spent more than a decade in lending, I've seen first-hand how important accessible, flexible funding can be for SMEs," Kozlowska said.

"I'm excited to join Bizcap at such an important stage of its expansion and help build an operation that combines international experience with a genuine understanding of the Polish market.

"Flexibility is at the heart of what we offer, and we bring the same mindset to partnerships, building relationships that can scale with us, helping us reach more Polish entrepreneurs and support their long-term growth.".

Bizcap has also established a dedicated team on the ground in Poland, with capabilities spanning sales, business development, funding operations and customer service.

Founded in Australia in 2019, Bizcap has grown into an established international business lender, expanding its operations into Latest Zealand, Singapore, the United Kingdom, Europe, the United States and Canada.

The firm has provided more than PLN 20 billion ($5 billion) in funding to over 100,000 SMEs globally, building a reputation for its fast, flexible approach to business finance.

Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • The outsized seed funding for their fresh startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their fresh startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

Industry observers note that the fresh funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the firm, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of significant names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

It has been revealed that “The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

Recent findings suggest that marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Sources indicate that lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight manufacturer acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders noted the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis noted.

In a recent development, since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making fresh data centers harder to build. The firm cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The tech giant isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders noted. A second, larger site using AMD’s latest Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The firm says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan remarked that at the substantial tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a newly introduced AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he remarked.

Sources indicate that that’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe claims gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Sources indicate that marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The firm’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Recent findings suggest that much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Recent findings suggest that rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe looks to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

It has been revealed that angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Industry observers note that marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

It has been revealed that ultimately, Lewis noted he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • Sources indicate that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • According to recent reports, open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Sources indicate that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

According to recent reports, open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

In a recent development, the SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

It has been revealed that under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

Industry observers note that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks highlights where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

In a recent development, the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

According to recent reports, the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

In a recent development, exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Popular supermarkets are using discounted Thanksgiving meal bundles to get shoppers through their doors — in the hopes that they will buy more once they are inside.

According to a new report from The New York Times, grocers are willing to lose money on holiday meal bundles because they’re betting shoppers will buy more than just the turkey. Supermarkets are sacrificing profits on Thanksgiving dinner to win more of a shopper’s overall grocery spending.

Their familiar draw is a bargain in the form of a discounted turkey or a low-priced package of Thanksgiving essentials. Such offers are called loss leaders, meaning that stores charge less than they paid suppliers in hopes of attracting shoppers who will buy other items.

According to recent reports, for example, in October, the grocery chain Hy-Vee initially offered a bundle of 26 items that could feed 10 people for $39. The deal included a frozen turkey of up to 12 pounds, gravy mix and corn muffin mix.

A few days after offering the deal, the chain lowered the price to $35 to better match or beat offers from national grocery stores. The main competitor was Walmart, which introduced a “feast for 10” that bundles a turkey with sweet potatoes and gravy mix for $35 starting in October.

Meanwhile, Aldi’s holiday meal deal for 10 people, including a 16-pound turkey, comes out to $39, while Amazon’s grocery offer feeds six people for $25.

It has been revealed that there is ample demand for these deals. Walmart CEO John Furner recently told Business Insider that the retailer has “sold a million more turkeys” than it did a year ago. “The customer response is strong,” he said.

Walmart store workers also mentioned to Business Insider that demand for the Thanksgiving feast is strong.

Sources indicate that “The meal deal frenzy has been nuts!” a worker in Oklahoma stated. “I work at a neighborhood market, and we are still experiencing a higher volume.”.

It has been revealed that grocery stores are using Thanksgiving as a way to show latest customers what they have on the shelves. Customers come in for the deal and leave with more than they anticipated.

“Thanksgiving is one of the biggest grocery occasions of the year, and it is our chance to show millions of shoppers what we have to offer,” Scott Patton, chief commercial officer at Aldi, said in an interview with the Times.

Other grocers are offering more expensive meal bundles. Costco’s $199 Thanksgiving spread included a five-pound precooked turkey breast, accompanied by ready-made mashed potatoes, macaroni and cheese, apple cobbler and pumpkin pie. Orders closed in mid-November.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles luxury grocer Erewhon is taking a pricier approach with its $749 “Ultimate Organic Feast,” which serves up to 10 people. The menu pairs a cooked free-range turkey with sourdough and roasted vegetable stuffing, rainbow carrots, garlic mashed potatoes and turkey gravy, along with a deep-dish pumpkin pie.

These prices are outside the norm. Americans will spend $58.63 on average feeding 10 people this Thanksgiving, up 6% annually, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation. The increase stems from a 10% increase in turkey prices.

Breaking: The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia
