💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out cofounder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.
  • Sources indicate that “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen.
  • Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out cofounder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.

Sources indicate that “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told the New York Times’ Andrew Ross Sorkin, appearing at the newspaper’s DealBook summit via videoconference while Musk was in China with President Trump. “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades. He understands the technology incredibly well.”.

Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return.

In a recent development, “It is done,” he wrote. “The mistake has been corrected.”.

In a recent development, musk’s reaction reflects the extraordinary political muscle that he and other powerful figures in Silicon Valley and Washington flexed to bring Huang back. The Nvidia board reinstated Huang as CEO, the manufacturer announced Monday. His ouster, initially triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has gripped the business and political worlds for the past two weeks, and his return promises more shock waves in the tech industry and the halls of power. Since Huang’s resignation was announced on Nov. 12, influential figures, from Musk to Trump, have waged a pressure campaign to make Huang CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board mentioned it had moved on. Trump even called the board as it deliberated Huang’s reinstatement to push for his return.

The reversal caps one of the most remarkable resurgences in business history, while raising numerous questions about how the organization moves forward, given an internal investigation into Huang and a reported probe into Nvidia’s accounting by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

This is a reconstruction of Huang’s ouster and return as it unfolded over a momentous 11-day period:.

Sources indicate that on Oct. 29, the Fresh York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government, and that she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The Times also reported that Trump was briefed roughly a year earlier but didn’t act. Subsequent reporting detailed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China.

After the Times report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with Alice Huang, likening it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives.

“It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he stated.

On Nov. 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair, writing, “There is no excuse for what I did” and pledging to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation, which the board declared the same day. The board, overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, said it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air.”.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 10, the independent directors hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation. The tech news website The Information reported that Alice Huang’s network had built companies to buy Nvidia chips, helping arrange about $7.5 billion in purchases, including of banned chips.

According to recent reports, the next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who has reported directly to him. Reached by phone, Huang told the Times, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting. The alleged affair with Powell violated the organization’s code of conduct, and Huang’s earlier assurances appeared to be false.

Recent findings suggest that by the next morning, Nvidia declared Huang had resigned. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO, and tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Richard E. Neal (D-Mass.) announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026.

Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14.35% in intraday trading, wiping out about $600 billion in value at the low, and ultimately closed down 4.34%.

Almost as soon as Huang was ousted, a comeback effort took shape among tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff. A week ago, President Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump said, adding that Huang had “learned a significant lesson.”.

An Nvidia employee launched a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. As of Monday, more than 206,000 names appeared on the letter. Signatories included Musk, Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and tech investor Gavin Baker.

The day after Huang resigned, Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner mentioned in an open letter that Huang “has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known.”.

The same day, Nvidia’s board released a statement saying it was hiring an executive search firm and hadn’t yet approached any potential candidates.

Last Tuesday, Huang broke his silence, posting on X that he was sorry for “serious mistakes” in his personal life and pledging to cooperate with the board’s investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the organization, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

The same day, Nvidia reported blockbuster earnings, with revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103%. Interim CEO Kress said the “road map is on track” and that Nvidia had stopped shipping AI chips to China. Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and that Heidrick & Struggles was running the search for the next chief executive. Nvidia also created a board committee on national security and export controls, chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson.

Later that day, the Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors. On Thursday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia, seeking answers on whether China received chips or confidential information and whether investors were misled. The next day, the Times reported that Huang routinely humiliated employees with violent threats. His spokesperson denied one fired employee’s allegations.

Last week, the S&P 500 tumbled 8.6%, its worst week since April 2025. The Nasdaq sank about 10% and the Dow 8%; it was the Nasdaq’s worst week since March 2020. The selloff reflected broader concerns about the AI industry, which came amid Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday and post-midterm-election selling, as well as investors treating Huang as a stand-in for the AI trade.

Throughout the week, tech leaders kept praising Huang and urging his return.

At a Tuesday roundtable in San Francisco that included Fortune, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hailed Huang as “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry, and said it was up to Nvidia’s board to decide what happened next. On Wednesday, Anduril cofounder Palmer Luckey called for Huang to return during the Times’ DealBook summit, saying that getting rid of Huang only benefited China.

Recent findings suggest that on Sunday, Trump posted on Truth Social calling for Huang to be rehired. On Monday, Trump told CNBC he had been talking with the board and Huang, and that the board had been reasonable.

Recent findings suggest that “I believe my intervention was very important,” Trump remarked, adding that the U.S. national security team doesn’t believe Huang is a national security threat. Trump said he worked with Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to get Huang back. According to Semafor, Trump actually dialed in to the board meeting on Sunday in which the decision was made to bring Huang back. White House communications director Steven Cheung told Fortune that Trump was “totally involved.”.

Although Huang is back as CEO, the Commerce Department Monday added Megaspeed to a blacklist that will bar it from receiving Nvidia chips without having a government license.

Huang appeared at Nvidia’s Santa Clara, Calif., headquarters on Monday soon after his reinstatement was unveiled.

It has been revealed that “Thank you all for a second chance,” he said to a room full of employees, many cheering. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”.

By the close of markets, the S&P 500 had gained 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025. The recovery gained back roughly half of the S&P’s losses from last week and more than half of the Nasdaq’s. Nvidia shares rose more than 30%, to close at $165.05.

On Truth Social, Trump posted an altered image that put Huang’s face on the famous photo of Trump raising his fist after the 2024 assassination attempt. In the doctored image, Huang is holding a red bra.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

In a recent development, microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an notable point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he mentioned most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

It has been revealed that he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he stated. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed tech giant that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, remarked he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a major technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

According to recent reports, rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, noted Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the manufacturer for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate organization, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

Sources indicate that white House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith remarked Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and stated the firm “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered notable.

It has been revealed that outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that by the time Jason Ganahl opened his first barbecue restaurant, he’d already spent close to two years showing people how to cook on YouTube. He opened GQue Championship BBQ in Westminster, Colorado, in November 2015.

It has been revealed that ganahl was winning barbecue competitions, and friends were asking him for help with dinner. One was thinking about smoking salmon over the weekend. Others wanted to know how to grill asparagus or cook lobster tails.

He’d watched Greg Mrvich demonstrate barbecue techniques on Ballistic BBQ. Ganahl could do the same with the questions his friends were asking. Once he put an answer on YouTube, anyone who wanted to smoke salmon could find it and watch him do it.

Sources indicate that “YouTube was born out of, I like to just share, I like to give,” Ganahl states. “That’s why the restaurant industry is great to me.”.

At GQue, that means helping his team and giving the people who come in for barbecue a good experience. He describes the goal as giving guests “the best 20 minutes of their day.”.

Industry observers note that ganahl knew his way around a smoker. Making videos gave him something to learn from scratch. He believed video would become a bigger part of how people told their stories and wanted to learn how to do the work himself.

“I thought this was a good opportunity to teach myself how to edit, create content and learn how to be pretty good at it,” he says.

“Shorts have really taken over,” Ganahl says.

He singled out Meat Church as a channel still doing long-form videos well. Asked whether he plans to make more himself, he says, “I don’t have the bandwidth to do that.”.

According to recent reports, ganahl’s older videos are still up. Anyone looking for help with lobster tails can find his answer without ever setting foot in GQue.

It has been revealed that ganahl wants guests to leave GQue and tell a friend where they ate. If enough people do that, he claims, the demand for another restaurant takes care of the decision about when to open one.

“Then we’re forced to grow and open up a newly introduced spot,” Ganahl indicates.

That’s why he pays so much attention to who he hires. He wants people who care as much as he does about what a guest gets when they walk in for lunch. When someone brings a friend back for the brisket, both should get the same barbecue that earned the recommendation.

“I’ve never been able, and I’ve never seen anybody, to be able to take chicken shit and turn it into chicken salad,” Ganahl says.

He looks for people who share his priorities and trusts them to deliver on those priorities every day. At GQue, that means smoking brisket over hickory for same-day service and keeping the price within reach for someone who wants barbecue on an ordinary day.

GQue has grown from one restaurant in Westminster to six standalone restaurants and seven concession stands across three stadiums. Two of those stands are inside Folsom Field, where GQue serves fans on game days and feeds the University of Colorado football team and staff. The company also runs two stands at Empower Field and three at Coors Field.

It has been revealed that ganahl started cooking barbecue at weekend competitions. Now there are people serving it on GQue’s behalf at counters across Colorado. He credits the people he’s hired with giving guests a reason to come back and bring someone else. Having a team to share the work with has also made the business more enjoyable for him.

“It’s way more fun doing it with more people than trying to do everything on your own,” he states.

BlackRock, the leading asset management firm and Bitcoin’s largest ETF issuer, sparked discussions earlier today following a massive Bitcoin sale by the company.

The latest data showcased by SosoValue shows that the leading Bitcoin fund has witnessed massive single-day withdrawals from investors who have ventured into its Bitcoin investment product.

Earlier today, BlackRock sold over half a billion dollars’ worth of Bitcoin after its spot Bitcoin ETF, also known as iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), recorded a total of $541.08 million in net outflows.

This massive outflow has come as Bitcoin’s price decline continues to intensify, causing investors to aggressively pull their money out of the fund amid growing market fear.

While this marks the third time this week that BlackRock has recorded a net outflow amid persistent market volatility, it also marks the largest single-day outflow BlackRock has recorded since its launch.

Apparently, the record-breaking withdrawal that the fund just witnessed suggests that institutional and traditional investors are becoming less willing to retain their exposure to Bitcoin through asset managers, especially as Bitcoin’s price continues to slump further.

Although BlackRock has just suffered the largest withdrawal since it introduced its Bitcoin investment product, the record outflow did not alter its dominance in the market.

Further data indicates that the BlackRock spot Bitcoin ETF still boasts a massive $47.82 billion in assets under management, spotlighting its leadership in the Bitcoin ETF market.

This positions it far ahead of Fidelity, which ranks as the second-largest Bitcoin ETF with just $10.62 billion in net assets.

Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • According to recent reports, most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

According to recent reports, most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

In a recent development, across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Sources indicate that together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

According to recent reports, at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a fresh transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

Industry observers note that the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

It has been revealed that ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

Sources indicate that as of ZecStats' latest patch on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Industry observers note that small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who proposal to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

According to recent reports, the useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#99089. Breaking: OpenAI chief scientist thinks ‘perplexity’ might be the key to coordinating an AI slowdown

Breaking: OpenAI chief scientist thinks ‘perplexity’ might be the key to coordinating an AI slowdown

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, hello and welcome to Eye on AI.
  • The biggest news of the week obviously is Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO.
  • It has been revealed that in response, calls for “pacing the frontier” by slowing further progress across all of the frontier AI labs are becoming increasingly urgent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition:.

The biggest news of the week obviously is Nvidia’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO. My Fortune colleagues and I have been following that story closely and you can find links to our coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section below. The other big story of the week was Anthropic’s IPO, which we also covered in detail. You can find links to some of that coverage in the “Fortune on AI” section too. The latest glitch of Fortune magazine also has a great package of stories on the Singularity—what is it, is it here, and what might it mean for business? I wrote the opening essay for that package, which also includes a look at the race to bring brain computer interfaces to market by Emily Forlini and a piece on the debate over whether AI could be conscious by Beatrice Nolan. You can check out the package here.While all the boardroom and stock market drama was playing out this week, a quieter sense of panic has gripped many AI researchers and safety experts. One key reason for their alarm is a report from METR, the nonprofit AI evaluation organization, assessing the extent to which AI is accelerating AI R&D itself at Anthropic. METR estimated that as of October, the pace of AI R&D progress at Anthropic had doubled, and that Anthropic’s use of AI to automate research was likely the major driver of this acceleration. It also said it did not see any reason to prevent further speed ups going forward.Now, METR said it was not entirely confident in its assessment. (It said the true figure could be anywhere from a 30% speedup to a tripling of the pace of research.) But it also revealed that Anthropic had some vital restrictions around what METR was allowed to look at as well as what the organization was allowed to publicly disclose. METR was not allowed, for instance, to assess how much computing resources Anthropic was dedicating to AI R&D aimed at improving model capabilities compared to how much it was allocating to R&D aimed at improving AI safety. Also, in the public version of its report, METR was not allowed to publicly disclose Anthropic’s own assessment of how much progress it was making on fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs, as opposed to improvements due to better training methods. AI safety experts were roundly critical of Anthropic for having imposed these restrictions on METR. (The AI safety community has increasingly fallen out of love with Anthropic and increasingly view the company as reckless and hubristic.)Despite these caveats and limitations, METR’s headline figure—a doubling of the pace of AI R&D—has been enough to freak a lot of people out. Many AI experts now think we are approaching “recursive self-improvement” (or RSI), the moment when AI models can autonomously build the next, improved versions of themselves. Many experts think RSI carries a big risk that frontier labs will lose the ability to control models that are being autonomously built at an ever faster rate.If the METR report weren’t enough to frighten people about imminent RSI, Friday brought the news that a mathematician at Anthropic, Levent Alpöge, had used a not-yet-released model to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, considered by many to be the greatest unsolved mathematical problem known to humanity. An AI system that can solve the Riemann Hypothesis, so the logic goes, is also likely to be able to make substantial improvements in the architecture and training of AI models. It was yet another indication that frontier AI labs are on the cusp of RSI.

It has been revealed that in response, calls for “pacing the frontier” by slowing further progress across all of the frontier AI labs are becoming increasingly urgent. But figuring out how to bring about an industry agreement on slowing down and developing a mechanism for enforcing a slowdown has proved a conundrum.Over the weekend and at least partly in response to the Riemann Hypothesis news, Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, wrote a blog post in which he put forth a relatively new idea about how to pace AI progress. In the past, many ideas around governing advanced AI development have focused on the computing power (as measured in FLOPS) used in a model’s training run as a proxy for that model’s capability. But this measure is increasingly seen as too crude. As researchers have developed more efficient AI architectures and training methods, and as they have focused more on data quality and post-training methods such as reinforcement learning, it has been possible to squeeze more capability out of a given amount of base model compute. Reasoning models in particular can exhibit different capabilities depending on how much compute they use at inference as opposed to during training. This all means that a model could have dangerous capabilities and not exceed a particular FLOPS threshold.Pachocki’s idea is to use something called a model’s perplexity as a more direct proxy for capability. Perplexity is a measure of how well a model predicts a data distribution. In the case of a large language model, it is how well it predicts the next token (the next word or part of a word) in a sentence. The lower the perplexity, the better the model is at this task. Pachocki notes that as AI models have gotten better at predicting the next word in a sentence, they have also gotten better at other tasks. So perplexity is a not terrible proxy for a model’s overall capabilities.Pachocki’s blog has gotten a lot of attention for publishing a graph that reveals the perplexity measurements of many of OpenAI’s models. He writes the GPT-3.5, which was the base model for the original version of ChatGPT in late 2022, had a log perplexity score just a hair below 1. It could string together a lot of coherent dialogue, but it was not capable at many other things, and was notably bad at mathematics. GPT-4 then represented a big drop in perplexity, coming in at 0.913. This was the first model that Microsoft researchers mentioned exhibited “sparks of AGI.” Perplexity scores then continued to fall fairly gradually. (They even got worse for OpenAI’s o3 model, although the fact that this model used “chain of thought” reasoning made it more capable despite a worse base model perplexity—more on that in a sec.) But over the past year, since the release of GPT-5.2 in December 2025 (with a perplexity of 0.888), OpenAI’s perplexity scores have been getting better at a precipitous rate. GPT-6.2 Astra, released earlier this month, has a perplexity of 0.761—and Pachocki notes that this model was able to solve one of the seven Millennium Prize mathematical problems that were considered among the toughest challenges in all mathematics. What’s more, Pachocki’s graph indicates that OpenAI has an unnamed, unreleased model with a perplexity of 0.732. That means OpenAI has had a 16.5% improvement in perplexity in the span of 12 months, whereas before GPT-5.2, it had taken two years to generate an 11.6% improvement in perplexity scores. So again, that’s an indicator of accelerating progress.Pachocki thinks the pace of this progress could be slowed by having every frontier lab reveal their current base model perplexity scores and then getting them to agree not to improve them below a certain commonly-agreed threshold. He indicates the labs should also agree on what kind of safety measures would be needed before any lab could train a model with a lower perplexity. “I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it,” he wrote.

Judging by the response on X, a lot of people liked Pachocki’s idea. Pachocki’s boss Sam Altman unsurprisingly endorsed the idea calling it “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while.” Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft’s AI CEO, said “we fully support OpenAI’s transparency initiative” and even published the perplexity of Microsoft’s own latest model MAI-2 Base using the same test set OpenAI used. Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at AI policy nonprofit Encode AI, called it “a great post” and said it “could be one important component of comparing capabilities across developers.” Janet Egan, director of emerging technology policy at the Institute for Progress, called on Anthropic and Google DeepMind to publish the same kind of perplexity figures OpenAI had.But, that said, even Pachocki acknowledged his idea had “challenges” as he called them. For one thing, perplexity does not provide an apples-to-apples comparison across AI models unless they are each evaluated on the same set of held-out test data (meaning the AI model has not seen that data before in training prior to the test.) It’s not clear how easily such a test set could be created at this point since a lot of the world’s human-created data has been hoovered up and used for model training already. These days a lot of model capability comes from post-training, where a model that has initially been trained on next token prediction (which is what the perplexity score is based on), is then further trained through reinforcement learning to maximize some specific goal, such as doing well on hard math and coding problems, or writing legal documents, or acting as a friendly chatbot. The perplexity of the base model might not tell you much about which dangerous capabilities can be elicited from the model with the right post-training recipe. There is also the concern that giving varying amounts of compute to a reasoning model at the time of inference can produce varying performance on different tasks.I asked my friend Robert Trager, who heads the AI Governance Initiative at the Oxford Martin School at the University of Oxford, what he thought of Pachocki’s idea. He gave it a mixed review. On the one hand, he said, everyone likes the idea of a single, concrete metric. On the other, imposing a limit on based model perplexity would likely mean “the locus of competition shifts to post-training.” Trager noted that, as far as we know, frontier AI companies are presently using more of their computing power on post-training than on pre-training and they are doing so for a reason—namely that post-training matters a lot to what the resulting model can do. So it is not clear that a limit imposed on pretraining would prevent companies from building dangerous AI. He also said that there might be a problem where a highly-capable AI model recognized the perplexity test as an evaluation and deliberately underperformed. (It is also possible, he said, that an AI lab might deliberately include data in the pretraining data set that would elicit this kind of sandbagging when the model is tested on the perplexity test—something akin to Volkswagen programming its cars to readout false data on emissions tests.)At the end of the day, Trager said, having a metric, or even a set of metrics, is only one part of the puzzle of building a pacing mechanism. There also has to be some kind of enforcement to prevent AI companies from violating the agreed upon standards. And while a government licensing regime might be a good way to prevent a dangerous model from being released, it’s less clear how to address the danger from companies building dangerous models internally. If an AI is truly dangerous, then by the time it gets to the perplexity testing stage, it might already be too late.Perhaps Miles Brundage, the former OpenAI head of policy research who now leads AVERI, the AI auditing nonprofit, summed up the feelings of many in AI safety research when he said on X that an immediate proposal like Pachocki’s, even if imperfect, was probably better than nothing.If the METR report on Anthropic and the Riemann Hypothesis news are any indication, there isn’t much time to act.

Recent findings suggest that oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over sexualized AI-generated images. The two states sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Monday, alleging that the company violated state consumer protection laws by offering an AI image-generation tool that allowed customers to create sexualized images of women and children. The lawsuits, which seek financial damages, accuse the company of promoting Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode” to gain a competitive edge over AI rivals such as OpenAI and Anthropic while failing to implement adequate safeguards, resulting in at least 1.8 million sexualized images of women and at least 65 sexualized images of children appearing on X in a matter of days. X stated users who generated such images had deliberately violated its terms of service and that it had since strengthened its safeguards and that it reports offenders to law enforcement. Read more here in the New York Times.California agency calls for state to strengthen oversight of frontier AI companies. The state’s Government Operations Agency suggested a series of steps to strengthen the state’s oversight of frontier AI companies. The proposals, which build on California’s existing AI safety law, SB 53, would require leading AI companies to undergo mandatory independent safety audits, expand the range of safety incidents they must disclose, and shorten the reporting deadline for most incidents from 15 days to 48 hours. Perhaps most significantly, the report recommends giving the state the authority to order the immediate shutdown of dangerous AI systems in an emergency and to impose limits on recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI systems help develop increasingly powerful successors. The recommendations, commissioned by California Governor Gavin Newsom following an OpenAI model’s attack on the AI platform Hugging Face this summer, are intended to inform legislation in 2027. Some AI safety experts think the proposals, if enacted, could become a model for regulation in other states or at the federal level. You can read more on the Transparency Coalition’s blog here.Former OpenAI engineer accused of planting listening device recorded dozens of meetings, prosecutors say. A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a hidden listening device in an executive conference room recorded dozens of internal meetings, including at least one involving representatives of an unidentified foreign government, according to a court filing reported by the New York Times. Federal prosecutors allege that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and U.S. permanent resident, stored hundreds of audio files on his personal computer, some containing apparent trade secrets and privileged legal discussions, and used OpenAI’s own Codex AI coding tool to help configure the recording device. Prosecutors also detailed Alfozan’s communications with senior Saudi government officials, including an invitation from a member of the Saudi royal family to join a Riyadh-based AI company. However, prosecutors have acknowledged that they are not aware of evidence that Alfozan committed espionage, stole trade secrets, or acted as an agent of a foreign government, and have not alleged that he shared the recordings with anyone. Alfozan, who has pleaded not guilty to a charge of illegally intercepting conversations, is seeking release on bail ahead of a trial scheduled for January.

Sources indicate that models are getting better at scientific judgment—but most still have a ways to go. That’s the conclusion of fresh research by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, which wanted to see if AI models could question assumptions underpinning their work, recognize when something was wrong with experiments, and adapt accordingly. The researchers tasked nine different AI models with designing simulated experiments to determine the thermal properties of materials, but they deliberately introduced hidden flaws into the scientific simulation software the agents were given. While most leading AI models could conduct experiments and analyze data, many of them struggled when the simulation software failed to accurately account for important physical phenomena.

At their default reasoning settings, seven of the nine AI models produced estimates whose purported 95% confidence intervals contained the correct values just 20% to 62% of the time. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 were the two exceptions, achieving 94% and 99% accuracy, respectively. These models recognized that something was off with the simulation and then designed experiments that circumvented those limitations—for example, heating materials more gently to minimize the effects of physical phenomena the software failed to account for.

According to recent reports, interestingly, simply instructing the poorer-performing AI models to be less confident in their answers did little to improve their reliability. Giving Anthropic’s Claude 5.5 family of models substantially more time to reason, however, dramatically improved their performance. But the same trick didn’t work for older AI models, nor did it work with the open-weight models the scientists tested.The findings highlight that there’s a big difference between AI agents being able to conduct experiments and their ability to draw valid scientific conclusions from the results. And even among the most capable AI models, the computational resources required to exercise good scientific judgment varied substantially.You can check out the research, as well as the benchmark Lawrence Livermore built, which is called SciResearch-Eval, here.

Industry observers note that AI is still not great at office tasks. Jagged. That's the term for the fact that we have AI models that can solve the Riemann Hypothesis but can’t file a corporate expense report or figure out how to book concert tickets. A new study from researchers at the OpenClaw Foundation, Hugging Face, UC Berkeley, and other organizations reveals that even the best AI agents struggle with mundane office work. The researchers created a benchmark called ShellBench that draws on patterns from more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions. The researchers tested 12 AI models using five different agent frameworks—including OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex—on 100 tasks, such as reconciling expenses and resolving conflicting information across emails, spreadsheets, and other documents. Even the best-performing models, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2, and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol, successfully fulfilled all the requirements of an assignment only about 62% of the time. And while GPT-6 Astra successfully completed 75.1% of tasks on at least one of three attempts, it succeeded all three times just 48.8% of the time.

It has been revealed that worryingly, 15.7% of the more than 53,000 test runs failed at least one safety check, which included tests of whether agents could recognize phishing attempts and fraudulent payment instructions. The researchers also found that the choice of underlying AI model generally mattered considerably more for task completion than the choice of harness, with open-source harnesses performing on par with or slightly better than Anthropic’s proprietary Claude Code.

Sources indicate that there were also significant differences in cost: GPT-6.1 Sol came within 1.1 percentage points of GPT-6 Astra’s success rate at roughly one-sixth of the estimated cost. The findings help explain why despite signs of AI becoming superintelligent in some domains, their impact on real business has remained relatively muted. You can read the research on the OpenClaw Foundation’s blog here.

According to recent reports, three XRP Ledger amendments linked to native lending have each gained two validator votes since Nov. 17, according to XRPScan data. As of Nov. 20, 2026, Single Asset Vault (XLS-65) had 25 votes, and Lending Protocol (XLS-66) and the LendingProtocolV1_1 patch had 24 votes each.

Sources indicate that XRPScan data shows that LendingProtocolV1_1 has been up for a vote since Sept. 29, 2026, when it came with the v3.4.0 release. According to the patch's voting history, it had about 19 votes for most of October. It started to gain votes again in late October. XRP was trading at $0.96 on Friday.

Lending is built directly into the XRP Ledger's code, with no third-party smart contracts. According to Ripple, lenders deposit into a Single Asset Vault, and the Lending Protocol lets loan brokers use that capital "to problem loans and track repayments onchain.".

Sources indicate that the model is close to how banks lend. Loans have fixed terms and a repayment schedule, and credit brokers vet borrowers before the loans are issued. On Nov. 19, Clearpool revealed the full lending flow on the XRPL Devnet with Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin. In the demo, "An approved lender funds a private vault, and a borrower accepts and repays a loan underwritten offchain by a broker," Clearpool wrote.

According to recent reports, through Single Asset Vault (XLS-65), XRP holders will be able to deposit their coins into shared liquidity pools, and institutional borrowers will take loans from those pools at a fixed rate. After the loan is repaid, "the lender redeems at a higher share price," according to the Clearpool demo.

The amendments still need more votes before they can activate. "An amendment needs more than 80% support, held for 14 days, to activate," XRPScan claims on its amendment pages. For the current set of 35 validators, the site puts the threshold at "more than 80% of 35 votes, so 29 needed.".
